genres.name: Hip-Hop / Trap
genres.summary: Drum pocket, sample mood, 808 tuning, vocal space and arrangement that leaves room for the artist.

zones.label: Thump
zones.tip: The kick's weight. In trap the 808 often owns the deep sub, so keep the kick's energy here and let the 808 sit around or below it.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Boxiness
zones.tip: Cardboard / boxy zone. A narrow 2-4 dB cut here usually cleans the kick up.

zones.label: Click
zones.tip: Beater attack. This is what makes the kick audible on phone speakers. Boost a little if it disappears next to the 808.

tips.eq:
High-pass around 25-30 Hz to remove rumble you can't hear.

Decide who owns the sub. If your 808 is long and heavy, keep the kick's energy at 50-80 Hz and its click at 3-5 kHz.

If it sounds like cardboard, cut 250-400 Hz. Trick: sweep a narrow boost slowly until it sounds ugly, then turn that boost into a cut.
tips.compression:
Often not needed: trap kicks are usually already-processed samples.

If it needs more punch: slow-ish attack (10-30 ms) so the transient gets through, fast release (50-100 ms), 2-4 dB of gain reduction.

A clipper or saturation is common for making the kick louder without losing punch.
tips.sidechain:
Sidechain the 808 to the kick so they don't clash: fast attack, 50-120 ms release, 2-6 dB of ducking.

Alternatives: program the 808 so it doesn't hit at the same moment as the kick, or tune the kick to the song's key.
tips.reverb:
Usually none. Keep the kick dry and centred.

If you want space, use a very short room on a send and high-pass the reverb return above ~300 Hz so it doesn't muddy the low end.
tips.delay: Rarely used on the kick. A delay throw on a single kick hit can work as a transition effect. Automate the send so it's only on that hit.
tips.gain:
Aim for peaks around -12 to -6 dBFS on this track before bus processing.

Kick and 808 are usually the loudest elements: balance them first, then build everything else around them.

zones.label: Body
zones.tip: Weight of the snare/clap. Boost slightly if it's thin, cut if it's boxy.

zones.label: Crack
zones.tip: Snap and crack. Trap claps are often bright already, so tame 3-4 kHz if it's piercing.

zones.label: Sizzle
zones.tip: Air and sizzle. A gentle high shelf adds shine; too much gets brittle.

tips.eq:
High-pass at 100-150 Hz, because the kick and 808 own the low end.

Find the body at 180-250 Hz and the crack at 2-5 kHz. Trap snares and claps are usually bright; if one pierces your ears, cut narrowly around 3-4 kHz.
tips.compression:
Fast attack softens the hit; slow attack (10-30 ms) emphasises the snap. 3-5 dB of reduction.

Parallel compression (blend in a heavily squashed copy) adds density without killing the transient.
tips.sidechain: Not usually needed. Sometimes ducking a dense loop or pad with the snare helps it punch through.
tips.reverb:
A short plate or room on a send: 0.8-1.5 s decay, 10-30 ms pre-delay. Keep it subtle in trap; boom-bap can take more room character.

High-pass the reverb return around 300-500 Hz.
tips.delay: Delay throws (1/8 or 1/4) on the last snare of a phrase. Filter the delay so it doesn't fight the vocal.
tips.gain: Peaks roughly -14 to -8 dBFS. The snare should be clearly heard but usually sits a touch under the kick.

zones.label: Sub
zones.tip: The 808's fundamental. Felt more than heard. Check it on headphones or a sub: laptop speakers can't play it.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Mud / overlap
zones.tip: Where the 808 overlaps the kick and other instruments. A small dip here tightens the low end.

zones.label: Harmonics
zones.tip: Makes the 808 audible on phones and earbuds. Create these with saturation/distortion rather than EQ boosts.
zones.tooLittle: Not enough {label}, so this will disappear on phones and laptops. Add saturation/distortion to create harmonics, or boost about {amt} dB around {hz}.

tips.eq:
High-pass around 25-30 Hz.

Make sure the 808 is tuned to the song's key. That matters more than EQ.

If it disappears on small speakers, add saturation to create harmonics instead of boosting the sub. Clean up overlap with the kick by dipping where the kick's thump lives, or use sidechain.

Trick: layer a sine an octave above the 808 so it stays audible on small speakers.
tips.compression:
808 samples are usually consistent already. Use light compression or a limiter/clipper to control peaks when notes vary in level.

Avoid very fast release on low frequencies (keep it above ~50 ms), or it will distort.
tips.sidechain:
Key move: sidechain the 808 to the kick with 2-6 dB of reduction and a short release so the kick punches through.

Or arrange the pattern so kick and 808 don't overlap.
tips.reverb: None. Reverb on sub frequencies creates mud. Keep the 808 mono and dry.
tips.delay: None on the sub. A filtered delay on a high-passed, saturated duplicate can add movement in a breakdown.
tips.gain:
The 808 is often the loudest reading in the whole mix: peaks around -10 to -4 dBFS on the track.

Watch that it doesn't eat all your master headroom. Leave ~6 dB on the master bus.

zones.label: Rumble
zones.tip: Handling noise, plosives and room rumble. High-pass up to ~100-120 Hz for rap vocals.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter (12-18 dB/oct) and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Muffled, boxy sound. Cut a few dB if the vocal sounds like it's in a cupboard.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Clarity and intelligibility. A gentle broad boost helps every word come through.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: Harsh S and T sounds live here. Use a de-esser instead of a static EQ cut.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} instead of a static EQ cut. Aim for 3-6 dB of reduction on the S's only.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Expensive-sounding sheen. A high shelf boost, added before the de-esser catches the extra S's.

tips.eq:
High-pass at 80-120 Hz (higher for rap than singing). Cut mud at 200-400 Hz if it sounds muffled.

Rap vocals need clarity: a gentle boost at 3-5 kHz for presence and a high shelf above 10 kHz for air.

Tame harsh S's with a de-esser (5-9 kHz) rather than EQ.
tips.compression:
Rap vocals are compressed hard so every word is audible.

Common setup, two stages:
1) A fast compressor (1176-style, 4:1, fast attack) catching peaks: 3-5 dB of reduction.
2) A smoother one (LA-2A-style) for 2-3 dB more.

6-10 dB total is normal in hip-hop.
tips.sidechain:
Optional: duck the beat by 1-3 dB when the vocal plays.

More transparent trick: a dynamic EQ dip at 2-4 kHz on the beat, triggered by the vocal.
tips.reverb:
Modern hip-hop vocals are dry and in-your-face. Use a short plate or room at low level, or reverb only on ad-libs and line endings.

High-pass the return at 300-500 Hz and low-pass it at 8-10 kHz.
tips.delay:
1/4 or 1/8 note delay throws on the last word of a line are a classic.

Put the delay on a send, filter it, and automate the send so only the words you choose echo.
tips.gain:
Record the vocal peaking around -12 to -6 dBFS into your chain.

In the mix the vocal should be the loudest mid-range element, on top of the beat.

zones.label: Clang / body
zones.tip: Low clang and body. Usually high-passed away so hats don't cloud the snare and kick.

zones.label: Harshness
zones.tip: Where hats get harsh and clash with vocals. Cut 1-3 dB if it pierces.
zones.tooMuch: There's {dev} dB more harshness than typical around {hz}. Try a dynamic EQ or a narrow cut of {amt} dB there, and compare with bypass.

zones.label: Sizzle
zones.tip: Shimmer and sparkle. A gentle shelf adds life; too much gets brittle.

tips.eq:
Trap hats run straight 8ths or 16ths with 1/16-1/32 and triplet rolls; boom bap hats swing (MPC-style ~54-58%). Vary velocity so they don't sound robotic.

High-pass hats at 300-600 Hz. If they're harsh, cut 1-3 dB around 2-5 kHz; for sparkle, a gentle shelf around 8-10 kHz. Low-pass at 15-18 kHz if they sound fizzy.
tips.compression: Hats rarely need compression. Shape them with velocity and transient shapers instead; light bus compression on all percussion can add glue.
tips.sidechain: Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump. Hats are usually left un-ducked so the groove stays steady.
tips.reverb: This genre keeps things fairly dry and upfront: use short rooms or plates at low level, and save bigger spaces for transitions and ear candy. Keep hat reverb short so it doesn't wash out the groove.
tips.delay: Short 1/16 or 1/8 delays (filtered, low level) create movement on percussion. Ping-pong delays widen hats without making them louder.
tips.gain: Hats and percussion peak around -20 to -12 dBFS. They're usually the quietest drum elements but the busiest.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Leads rarely need this range. High-pass it so the kick and bass stay clean.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up. Cut if the lead sounds cloudy or masks the chords.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Where a lead cuts through. Watch for clashes with the vocal here.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Brightness and shine. Supersaws and plucks live up here too.

tips.eq:
Trap melodies are dark and minor: bells, plucks, flutes, piano or choir. Keep them simple so the vocal has space.

High-pass at 150-300 Hz (higher if there's a lot going on in the low mids). Find the presence at 1-4 kHz, and if a vocal is present, cut the lead a little where the vocal is strongest.
tips.compression: Synths are already consistent, so compression is optional. Use it for density or saturation for harmonics. OTT-style multiband compression is common in EDM leads.
tips.sidechain: Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump.
tips.reverb: This genre keeps things fairly dry and upfront: use short rooms or plates at low level, and save bigger spaces for transitions and ear candy.
tips.delay: Tempo-synced delays (1/8, dotted 1/8 or 1/4) on a send. Filter the returns and duck them under the dry lead so the melody stays clear.
tips.gain: Leads peak around -16 to -9 dBFS. They should be clearly heard but sit under the vocal if there is one.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Pads and chords rarely need this. High-pass at 150-300 Hz so kick and bass own the low end.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: The most common mix problem: chords piling up in the low mids. Keep it tidy.

zones.label: Body
zones.tip: The warmth of the chords. Enough to fill, not so much it masks vocals and leads.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Shimmer and width. A gentle shelf can make pads feel expensive.

tips.eq:
Chords are usually a dark minor loop (or a chopped soul sample in boom bap) that leaves room for the rapper.

High-pass pads and chords at 150-300 Hz, cut mud at 200-500 Hz, and consider a low-pass around 10 kHz on dark pads so they don't fight hats and vocals.
tips.compression: Usually not needed on pads. For stabs, light compression or saturation adds punch. OTT can brighten supersaw chords.
tips.sidechain: Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump.
tips.reverb: This genre keeps things fairly dry and upfront: use short rooms or plates at low level, and save bigger spaces for transitions and ear candy. Pads can take more reverb than anything else in the mix.
tips.delay: Stereo or ping-pong delays widen chord stabs. Filter and duck them.
tips.gain: Chords and pads peak around -18 to -10 dBFS. They support; they're rarely the loudest element.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Rumble and boom. High-pass so the bass owns the low end.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Honk
zones.tip: Honky, boxy piano tone. Cut 2-4 dB if it sounds cheap.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Definition. A small dip here makes room for the vocal.

zones.label: Brilliance
zones.tip: Sparkle on the hammers. A gentle boost for brightness.

tips.eq:
Piano and Rhodes carry many beats. Keep them out of the vocal's 2-5 kHz range.

In a busy mix, high-pass piano at 100-200 Hz, cut honk at 500 Hz-1 kHz, and dip 2-4 kHz slightly so the vocal owns the presence range. Boost 5-8 kHz for brilliance.
tips.compression: Gentle compression (2-4 dB, medium attack) evens out dynamics. Keep it light on expressive parts.
tips.sidechain: Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump.
tips.reverb: This genre keeps things fairly dry and upfront: use short rooms or plates at low level, and save bigger spaces for transitions and ear candy.
tips.delay: Subtle delays add depth; long filtered delays suit ambient and lo-fi keys.
tips.gain: Keys peak around -16 to -9 dBFS depending on how central they are to the track.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Rumble and boom. High-pass so the bass stays clear.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Boom / mud
zones.tip: Boominess and boxiness. Cut 2-4 dB if the guitar masks the bass or vocal.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Pick attack and definition. Where a guitar cuts through.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Shimmer and string sparkle, especially on acoustics.

tips.eq:
Guitar loops are common in melodic trap: high-pass them and roll off the top so they sit behind the vocal.

High-pass at 80-100 Hz (acoustics from 60 Hz; push higher until it thins, then back off). Cut 200-500 Hz if it's boomy; add presence at 1.5-5 kHz and air at 8-12 kHz.
tips.compression: Light compression (2-4 dB) for strummed parts; more for funky, rhythmic riffs.
tips.sidechain: Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump.
tips.reverb: This genre keeps things fairly dry and upfront: use short rooms or plates at low level, and save bigger spaces for transitions and ear candy.
tips.delay: Slapback or tempo delays add space; long delays and volume swells create ambient textures.
tips.gain: Guitars peak around -16 to -9 dBFS.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Backing vocals and chops don't need this. High-pass at 150-300 Hz.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up from stacked vocals. Cut to keep the lead clear.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Keep backing parts a little softer here than the lead vocal.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: Stacked S's get loud fast. De-ess backing vocals harder than the lead.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} rather than a static EQ cut.

tips.eq:
Ad-libs and doubles sit behind the lead: pan them, filter them and keep them quieter than the main vocal.

High-pass backing vocals and chops at 150-300 Hz, cut mud at 200-400 Hz, and keep them slightly darker than the lead so it stays in front.
tips.compression: Compress harder than the lead (6-10 dB) so stacks stay even and sit behind it.
tips.sidechain: Duck backing vocals 1-3 dB under the lead vocal if they compete. Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump.
tips.reverb: This genre keeps things fairly dry and upfront: use short rooms or plates at low level, and save bigger spaces for transitions and ear candy. Backing parts can take more reverb than the lead, which pushes them behind it.
tips.delay: Filtered stereo delays widen chops and harmonies. Keep them lower than the lead's delay.
tips.gain: Backing vocals and chops peak around -18 to -10 dBFS, below the lead vocal.

zones.label: Sub
zones.tip: The deepest low end of the whole mix. Check it on headphones or a sub, and keep it mono.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up across the whole mix: the most common reason mixes sound cloudy.

zones.label: Harshness
zones.tip: Where whole mixes get harsh and tiring. Fix it on the channels if you can.
zones.tooMuch: There's {dev} dB more harshness than typical around {hz}. Try a dynamic EQ or a narrow cut of {amt} dB there, and compare with bypass.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Top-end openness of the mix.

tips.eq:
Hip-hop masters are loud and bass-heavy, but the 808 must not distort the master.

On the mix bus, EQ in small moves (0.5-2 dB, wide shapes). If one zone needs more than that, fix it on the channel that causes it. Keep everything below about 120 Hz mono.
tips.compression: Mix-bus glue: a slow attack (10-30 ms), auto or 100-300 ms release, ratio 1.5:1-2:1 and only 1-2 dB of gain reduction.
tips.sidechain: Not used on the master. Do sidechain and ducking on the individual channels.
tips.reverb: No reverb on the mix bus. Space belongs on the sends.
tips.delay: No delay on the mix bus.
tips.gain:
Before mastering, leave about 3-6 dB of headroom: peaks around -6 to -3 dBFS on the mix bus, with no limiter.

Typical master loudness for this genre: about -10 to -7 LUFS integrated, with true peak at -1 dBTP or lower.

Streaming services turn loud masters down: Spotify plays at about -14 LUFS by default (-11 LUFS in its 'loud' mode), Apple Music at about -16 LUFS. So mastering louder than the genre needs only costs you punch. Compare with a level-matched reference.

workflow.title: Genre map
workflow.text: Tempo: Boom bap 80-100 BPM · trap 130-160 BPM (often ~140) with a half-time feel. The goal: drum pocket, sample mood, 808 tuning, vocal space and arrangement that leaves room for the artist. Decide what job each section has before reaching for processors.

workflow.title: Reference listening
workflow.text: Pick two references: one for groove and one for mix tone. Level-match them before judging your track.

workflow.title: Session template
workflow.text: Create groups for drums, bass, music, hook/vocal and FX. Add a reference track and two sends before writing.

workflow.title: Core rhythm
workflow.text: Build the groove around sample chops and boom bap or trap drums. Keep it simple until the pocket works.

workflow.title: Drum sound choice
workflow.text: Choose kick, snare/clap and hats by role. Tune or swap before stacking processing.

workflow.title: Bass foundation
workflow.text: Use the kick and 808 relationship (tune the 808 to the key) as the low-end anchor. Make the note length and rhythm serve the kick.

workflow.title: Hook identity
workflow.text: Use the sample, trap hats or a hook lift as the part people remember. Mute it to test whether the track loses identity.

workflow.title: Arrangement sketch
workflow.text: Duplicate the loop across a timeline, then remove elements for intro, breakdown, build, drop/chorus and outro.

workflow.title: Energy curve
workflow.text: Use density, filter movement, automation and drum fills to create lift. Avoid adding layers just because a section feels empty.

workflow.title: Transition design
workflow.text: Use reverse tails, short fills, risers, mutes and reverb throws. A transition should explain the next section.

workflow.title: Kick and bass balance
workflow.text: Set kick and bass before mixing anything else. If these fight, no amount of mastering will save the track.

workflow.title: Sidechain or ducking
workflow.text: Use sidechain only where it creates space or groove. Set release musically, not just visually.

workflow.title: EQ cleanup
workflow.text: High-pass support parts, cut mud in context, and protect the midrange that carries the hook.

workflow.title: Compression
workflow.text: Use compression for control, groove and density. If the part gets smaller, slow the attack or reduce gain reduction.

workflow.title: Saturation
workflow.text: Add harmonics where the part needs to translate on smaller speakers. Gain-match before deciding it sounds better.

workflow.title: Stereo width
workflow.text: Keep the foundation centred. Put width in pads, textures, FX, doubles and support layers.

workflow.title: Reverb
workflow.text: Short spaces add placement. Long spaces add drama. Automate sends so the drop/groove stays focused.

workflow.title: Delay
workflow.text: Use timed delays for call-and-response, vocal chops, fills and ear candy. Filter delay returns to avoid clutter.

workflow.title: Automation pass
workflow.text: Automate one thing per section: filter, send, mute, width, distortion, pitch or macro movement.

workflow.title: Sound design resampling
workflow.text: Print sample chop moments to audio so the arrangement becomes editable and stable.

workflow.title: Vocal or sample space
workflow.text: Leave a pocket for the lead element. If vocals are coming later, mix the beat with that space protected.

workflow.title: Bus processing
workflow.text: Process groups lightly. Drums can take clip/saturation; music can take glue; FX returns can take EQ and ducking.

workflow.title: Loudness prep
workflow.text: Don't chase loudness until the low end and arrangement are stable. Loud masters expose weak balance.

workflow.title: Export checklist
workflow.text: Export the full mix, an instrumental where useful, and a rough master. Name files with BPM, key and version.

workflow.title: Phone check
workflow.text: The groove, hook and vocal space should survive on a phone. Add harmonics if the bass disappears.

workflow.title: Mono check
workflow.text: Collapse to mono and listen for missing hooks or weak drums. Fix phase before widening.

workflow.title: Beginner mistakes
workflow.text: Too many layers, too much reverb, no arrangement contrast, and mixing before the core idea works.

workflow.title: Practice drill
workflow.text: Make a 90-second Hip Hop sketch using only drums, 808, one sample or hook and two automation moves.

workflow.title: Advanced drill
workflow.text: Build a second version focused on verse space and compare which arrangement keeps energy better.

workflow.title: Release habit
workflow.text: Finish a rough version, write three notes, fix those only, then move on. Completion builds taste faster than endless tweaking.

theory.bpm: Boom bap 80-100 BPM · trap 130-160 BPM (often ~140) with a half-time feel
theory.groove:
Trap: snare/clap on beat 3 of each bar so the drums feel half-time while hi-hats run at full speed. Hats on 8ths or 16ths with 1/16, 1/32 and triplet rolls, velocity varied, and the occasional open hat choked by the next closed hat.
Boom bap: kick and snare backbeat (snare on 2 and 4) with extra 16th-note kicks, swung with MPC-style swing. Around 54-58% is the classic hip-hop range; 50% is straight, 66% is full triplet swing.
theory.keys: Trap is overwhelmingly minor: C, D, F#, G and A minor are common. Natural minor and harmonic minor cover most of it; Phrygian (minor with a flat 2nd) gives an extra-dark sound.
theory.tips: Tune the 808 to the key and let it follow the chord roots. Layering a sine an octave above the 808 helps it cut through on small speakers. Use fewer hi-hat rolls than you think: steady hats with a roll at the end of a phrase hit harder.

genres.theoryText:
TEMPO
Boom bap 80-100 BPM · trap 130-160 BPM (often ~140) with a half-time feel

GROOVE & DRUMS
Trap: snare/clap on beat 3 of each bar so the drums feel half-time while hi-hats run at full speed. Hats on 8ths or 16ths with 1/16, 1/32 and triplet rolls, velocity varied, and the occasional open hat choked by the next closed hat.
Boom bap: kick and snare backbeat (snare on 2 and 4) with extra 16th-note kicks, swung with MPC-style swing. Around 54-58% is the classic hip-hop range; 50% is straight, 66% is full triplet swing.

KEYS & SCALES
Trap is overwhelmingly minor: C, D, F#, G and A minor are common. Natural minor and harmonic minor cover most of it; Phrygian (minor with a flat 2nd) gives an extra-dark sound.

COMMON PROGRESSIONS
•  i - bVI - bVII   (Cm - Ab - Bb)  trap minor
•  i - bIII - bVI - bVII   (Cm - Eb - Ab - Bb)  dark trap
•  i - iv - i - bVI   (Am - Dm - Am - F)  boom bap
•  i - bVII - bVI - V   (Am - G - F - E)  Andalusian cadence, dark and cinematic
•  I - bVII - IV - I   (C - Bb - F - C)  soul loop, warm 90s feel

PRODUCTION TIPS
Tune the 808 to the key and let it follow the chord roots. Layering a sine an octave above the 808 helps it cut through on small speakers. Use fewer hi-hat rolls than you think: steady hats with a roll at the end of a phrase hit harder.

LOUDNESS
Typical master: about -10 to -7 LUFS integrated, true peak -1 dBTP or lower.

genres.name: Lo-Fi Hip Hop
genres.summary: Dusty drums, warm samples, relaxed swing, soft transients, tape tone and intimate arrangement.

zones.label: Thump
zones.tip: Soft, round weight. Lo-fi kicks are warm, not hard.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Boxiness
zones.tip: Some boxiness is part of the dusty sound, but too much gets muddy.

zones.label: Click
zones.tip: Lo-fi kicks have soft transients: this zone is usually rolled off.

tips.eq:
Dusty drums: high-pass at 30-40 Hz and low-pass the whole drum group around 6-10 kHz for that rolled-off, vintage tone.

Keep the kick round at 45-80 Hz and soften the click at 2.5-5 kHz.
tips.compression: Gentle compression with a slow attack, or tape saturation instead: it softens transients naturally. Soft transients are part of the sound.
tips.sidechain: A light duck (1-3 dB) of the chords or sample from the kick helps the groove breathe. Keep it subtle.
tips.reverb: A small room on the drum bus (the guides' 'small-room mix'): short, darker, low level.
tips.delay: Not used on the kick.
tips.gain: Peaks around -12 to -7 dBFS. Lo-fi is mellow; leave lots of headroom.

zones.label: Body
zones.tip: Warm body. Lo-fi snares are soft and thick.

zones.label: Crack
zones.tip: Keep crack soft. Harsh snares break the mood.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Usually rolled off for a vintage tone.

tips.eq:
Soft, dusty snares: high-pass at 100-150 Hz, keep body at 150-250 Hz, tame the crack at 2-5 kHz and low-pass above 8-10 kHz.

Rim shots and brushed snares fit the jazz feel.
tips.compression: Light (2-3 dB). Tape or vinyl saturation on the drum bus gives glue without squashing.
tips.sidechain: Not needed.
tips.reverb: Small, dark room or a lo-fi spring. Keep it intimate rather than big.
tips.delay: Occasional tape-style delays with wobble on the last snare of a loop.
tips.gain: Peaks around -14 to -9 dBFS.

zones.label: Fundamental
zones.tip: Muted, round bass notes. Warm but not boomy.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Lo-fi mixes get cloudy fast. Keep this tidy.

zones.label: Definition
zones.tip: Gentle note definition. Lo-fi bass is soft, so not too much.
zones.tooLittle: Not enough {label}, so this will disappear on phones and laptops. Add saturation/distortion to create harmonics, or boost about {amt} dB around {hz}.

tips.eq: The muted bass is the low-end anchor: a round, upright-style or soft synth bass. High-pass at 30 Hz, low-pass around 1-2 kHz for that muted tone, and cut mud at 150-300 Hz.
tips.compression: Gentle, slow compression or tape saturation for warmth and consistency.
tips.sidechain: A light duck (1-3 dB) from the kick keeps the low end clear.
tips.reverb: Keep it dry.
tips.delay: Not used.
tips.gain: Peaks around -12 to -7 dBFS.

zones.label: Rumble
zones.tip: High-pass up to ~150 Hz to remove rumble and plosives.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter (12-18 dB/oct) and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Muffled, boxy zone. Cut a few dB if the vocal lacks clarity.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Keep presence soft so the vocal sits inside the warm mix.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: Harsh S's live here. De-ess rather than EQ.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} instead of a static EQ cut. Aim for 3-6 dB of reduction on the S's only.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Lo-fi vocals and samples are usually rolled off up here for a vintage feel.

tips.eq: Lo-fi vocals are often samples, hums or soft spoken parts. High-pass at 150-250 Hz and low-pass at 6-8 kHz for a vintage, telephone-ish tone.
tips.compression: Gentle (3-5 dB), plus tape saturation for warmth.
tips.sidechain: Not usually needed.
tips.reverb: Small, dark rooms or lo-fi plates. Intimacy over size.
tips.delay: Tape delays with wobble (modulated) are part of the style. Filter the repeats darker.
tips.gain: Peaks around -14 to -8 dBFS.

zones.label: Clang / body
zones.tip: Low clang and body. Usually high-passed away so hats don't cloud the snare and kick.

zones.label: Harshness
zones.tip: Where hats get harsh and clash with vocals. Cut 1-3 dB if it pierces.
zones.tooMuch: There's {dev} dB more harshness than typical around {hz}. Try a dynamic EQ or a narrow cut of {amt} dB there, and compare with bypass.

zones.label: Sizzle
zones.tip: Shimmer and sparkle. A gentle shelf adds life; too much gets brittle.

tips.eq:
Hats are soft, dusty and swung (55-65%). Low-pass them and keep velocities varied.

High-pass hats at 300-600 Hz. If they're harsh, cut 1-3 dB around 2-5 kHz; for sparkle, a gentle shelf around 8-10 kHz. Low-pass at 15-18 kHz if they sound fizzy.
tips.compression: Hats rarely need compression. Shape them with velocity and transient shapers instead; light bus compression on all percussion can add glue.
tips.sidechain: Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump. Hats are usually left un-ducked so the groove stays steady.
tips.reverb: Keep spaces small and controlled: short rooms and plates (0.5-1.2 s), high-passed at 200-400 Hz. Keep hat reverb short so it doesn't wash out the groove.
tips.delay: Short 1/16 or 1/8 delays (filtered, low level) create movement on percussion. Ping-pong delays widen hats without making them louder.
tips.gain: Hats and percussion peak around -20 to -12 dBFS. They're usually the quietest drum elements but the busiest.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Leads rarely need this range. High-pass it so the kick and bass stay clean.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up. Cut if the lead sounds cloudy or masks the chords.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Where a lead cuts through. Watch for clashes with the vocal here.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Brightness and shine. Supersaws and plucks live up here too.

tips.eq:
Leads are mellow: soft keys, muted guitar or a hummed line. Avoid bright synths.

High-pass at 150-300 Hz (higher if there's a lot going on in the low mids). Find the presence at 1-4 kHz, and if a vocal is present, cut the lead a little where the vocal is strongest.
tips.compression: Synths are already consistent, so compression is optional. Use it for density or saturation for harmonics. OTT-style multiband compression is common in EDM leads.
tips.sidechain: Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump.
tips.reverb: Keep spaces small and controlled: short rooms and plates (0.5-1.2 s), high-passed at 200-400 Hz.
tips.delay: Tempo-synced delays (1/8, dotted 1/8 or 1/4) on a send. Filter the returns and duck them under the dry lead so the melody stays clear.
tips.gain: Leads peak around -16 to -9 dBFS. They should be clearly heard but sit under the vocal if there is one.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Pads and chords rarely need this. High-pass at 150-300 Hz so kick and bass own the low end.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: The most common mix problem: chords piling up in the low mids. Keep it tidy.

zones.label: Body
zones.tip: The warmth of the chords. Enough to fill, not so much it masks vocals and leads.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Shimmer and width. A gentle shelf can make pads feel expensive.

tips.eq:
Jazz 7th and 9th chords (maj7, m7, m9) are the core of the genre. Each chord usually lasts a bar or more.

High-pass pads and chords at 150-300 Hz, cut mud at 200-500 Hz, and consider a low-pass around 10 kHz on dark pads so they don't fight hats and vocals.
tips.compression: Usually not needed on pads. For stabs, light compression or saturation adds punch. OTT can brighten supersaw chords.
tips.sidechain: Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump.
tips.reverb: Keep spaces small and controlled: short rooms and plates (0.5-1.2 s), high-passed at 200-400 Hz. Pads can take more reverb than anything else in the mix.
tips.delay: Stereo or ping-pong delays widen chord stabs. Filter and duck them.
tips.gain: Chords and pads peak around -18 to -10 dBFS. They support; they're rarely the loudest element.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Rumble and boom. High-pass so the bass owns the low end.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Honk
zones.tip: Honky, boxy piano tone. Cut 2-4 dB if it sounds cheap.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Definition. A small dip here makes room for the vocal.

zones.label: Brilliance
zones.tip: Sparkle on the hammers. A gentle boost for brightness.

tips.eq:
Rhodes, felt piano and old samples are the main sound. Add tape wobble and roll off the highs.

In a busy mix, high-pass piano at 100-200 Hz, cut honk at 500 Hz-1 kHz, and dip 2-4 kHz slightly so the vocal owns the presence range. Boost 5-8 kHz for brilliance.
tips.compression: Gentle compression (2-4 dB, medium attack) evens out dynamics. Keep it light on expressive parts.
tips.sidechain: Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump.
tips.reverb: Keep spaces small and controlled: short rooms and plates (0.5-1.2 s), high-passed at 200-400 Hz.
tips.delay: Subtle delays add depth; long filtered delays suit ambient and lo-fi keys.
tips.gain: Keys peak around -16 to -9 dBFS depending on how central they are to the track.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Rumble and boom. High-pass so the bass stays clear.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Boom / mud
zones.tip: Boominess and boxiness. Cut 2-4 dB if the guitar masks the bass or vocal.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Pick attack and definition. Where a guitar cuts through.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Shimmer and string sparkle, especially on acoustics.

tips.eq:
Clean jazz guitar and muted plucks fit well. Low-pass and saturate for a vintage tone.

High-pass at 80-100 Hz (acoustics from 60 Hz; push higher until it thins, then back off). Cut 200-500 Hz if it's boomy; add presence at 1.5-5 kHz and air at 8-12 kHz.
tips.compression: Light compression (2-4 dB) for strummed parts; more for funky, rhythmic riffs.
tips.sidechain: Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump.
tips.reverb: Keep spaces small and controlled: short rooms and plates (0.5-1.2 s), high-passed at 200-400 Hz.
tips.delay: Slapback or tempo delays add space; long delays and volume swells create ambient textures.
tips.gain: Guitars peak around -16 to -9 dBFS.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Backing vocals and chops don't need this. High-pass at 150-300 Hz.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up from stacked vocals. Cut to keep the lead clear.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Keep backing parts a little softer here than the lead vocal.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: Stacked S's get loud fast. De-ess backing vocals harder than the lead.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} rather than a static EQ cut.

tips.eq:
Vocal snippets are filtered, pitched and drowned in texture.

High-pass backing vocals and chops at 150-300 Hz, cut mud at 200-400 Hz, and keep them slightly darker than the lead so it stays in front.
tips.compression: Compress harder than the lead (6-10 dB) so stacks stay even and sit behind it.
tips.sidechain: Duck backing vocals 1-3 dB under the lead vocal if they compete. Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump.
tips.reverb: Keep spaces small and controlled: short rooms and plates (0.5-1.2 s), high-passed at 200-400 Hz. Backing parts can take more reverb than the lead, which pushes them behind it.
tips.delay: Filtered stereo delays widen chops and harmonies. Keep them lower than the lead's delay.
tips.gain: Backing vocals and chops peak around -18 to -10 dBFS, below the lead vocal.

zones.label: Sub
zones.tip: The deepest low end of the whole mix. Check it on headphones or a sub, and keep it mono.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up across the whole mix: the most common reason mixes sound cloudy.

zones.label: Harshness
zones.tip: Where whole mixes get harsh and tiring. Fix it on the channels if you can.
zones.tooMuch: There's {dev} dB more harshness than typical around {hz}. Try a dynamic EQ or a narrow cut of {amt} dB there, and compare with bypass.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Top-end openness of the mix.

tips.eq:
Lo-fi masters stay softer and warmer than most genres. Don't crush it; the relaxed feel needs dynamics.

On the mix bus, EQ in small moves (0.5-2 dB, wide shapes). If one zone needs more than that, fix it on the channel that causes it. Keep everything below about 120 Hz mono.
tips.compression: Mix-bus glue: a slow attack (10-30 ms), auto or 100-300 ms release, ratio 1.5:1-2:1 and only 1-2 dB of gain reduction.
tips.sidechain: Not used on the master. Do sidechain and ducking on the individual channels.
tips.reverb: No reverb on the mix bus. Space belongs on the sends.
tips.delay: No delay on the mix bus.
tips.gain:
Before mastering, leave about 3-6 dB of headroom: peaks around -6 to -3 dBFS on the mix bus, with no limiter.

Typical master loudness for this genre: about -14 to -10 LUFS integrated, with true peak at -1 dBTP or lower.

Streaming services turn loud masters down: Spotify plays at about -14 LUFS by default (-11 LUFS in its 'loud' mode), Apple Music at about -16 LUFS. So mastering louder than the genre needs only costs you punch. Compare with a level-matched reference.

workflow.title: Genre map
workflow.text: Tempo: 70-90 BPM. The goal: dusty drums, warm samples, relaxed swing, soft transients, tape tone and intimate arrangement. Decide what job each section has before reaching for processors.

workflow.title: Reference listening
workflow.text: Pick two references: one for groove and one for mix tone. Level-match them before judging your track.

workflow.title: Session template
workflow.text: Create groups for drums, bass, music, hook/vocal and FX. Add a reference track and two sends before writing.

workflow.title: Core rhythm
workflow.text: Build the groove around dusty drums, jazz chords and vinyl texture. Keep it simple until the pocket works.

workflow.title: Drum sound choice
workflow.text: Choose kick, snare/clap and hats by role. Tune or swap before stacking processing.

workflow.title: Bass foundation
workflow.text: Use a muted, round bass as the low-end anchor. Make the note length and rhythm serve the kick.

workflow.title: Hook identity
workflow.text: Use jazz chords, tape wobble or a sample as the part people remember. Mute it to test whether the track loses identity.

workflow.title: Arrangement sketch
workflow.text: Duplicate the loop across a timeline, then remove elements for intro, breakdown, build, drop/chorus and outro.

workflow.title: Energy curve
workflow.text: Use density, filter movement, automation and drum fills to create lift. Avoid adding layers just because a section feels empty.

workflow.title: Transition design
workflow.text: Use reverse tails, short fills, risers, mutes and reverb throws. A transition should explain the next section.

workflow.title: Kick and bass balance
workflow.text: Set kick and bass before mixing anything else. If these fight, no amount of mastering will save the track.

workflow.title: Sidechain or ducking
workflow.text: Use sidechain only where it creates space or groove. Set release musically, not just visually.

workflow.title: EQ cleanup
workflow.text: High-pass support parts, cut mud in context, and protect the midrange that carries the hook.

workflow.title: Compression
workflow.text: Use compression for control, groove and density. If the part gets smaller, slow the attack or reduce gain reduction.

workflow.title: Saturation
workflow.text: Add harmonics where the part needs to translate on smaller speakers. Gain-match before deciding it sounds better.

workflow.title: Stereo width
workflow.text: Keep the foundation centred. Put width in pads, textures, FX, doubles and support layers.

workflow.title: Reverb
workflow.text: Short spaces add placement. Long spaces add drama. Automate sends so the drop/groove stays focused.

workflow.title: Delay
workflow.text: Use timed delays for call-and-response, vocal chops, fills and ear candy. Filter delay returns to avoid clutter.

workflow.title: Automation pass
workflow.text: Automate one thing per section: filter, send, mute, width, distortion, pitch or macro movement.

workflow.title: Sound design resampling
workflow.text: Print loop variation moments to audio so the arrangement becomes editable and stable.

workflow.title: Vocal or sample space
workflow.text: Leave a pocket for the lead element. If vocals are coming later, mix the beat with that space protected.

workflow.title: Bus processing
workflow.text: Process groups lightly. Drums can take clip/saturation; music can take glue; FX returns can take EQ and ducking.

workflow.title: Loudness prep
workflow.text: Don't chase loudness until the low end and arrangement are stable. Loud masters expose weak balance.

workflow.title: Export checklist
workflow.text: Export the full mix, an instrumental where useful, and a rough master. Name files with BPM, key and version.

workflow.title: Phone check
workflow.text: The groove, hook and vocal space should survive on a phone. Add harmonics if the bass disappears.

workflow.title: Mono check
workflow.text: Collapse to mono and listen for missing hooks or weak drums. Fix phase before widening.

workflow.title: Beginner mistakes
workflow.text: Too many layers, too much reverb, no arrangement contrast, and mixing before the core idea works.

workflow.title: Practice drill
workflow.text: Make a 90-second Lo-Fi sketch using only drums, bass, one chord loop and two automation moves.

workflow.title: Advanced drill
workflow.text: Build a second version focused on ambient noise and texture and compare which arrangement keeps energy better.

workflow.title: Release habit
workflow.text: Finish a rough version, write three notes, fix those only, then move on. Completion builds taste faster than endless tweaking.

genres.theoryText:
TEMPO
70-90 BPM

GROOVE & DRUMS
Swung boom bap: kick and snare like 90s hip-hop (snare on 2 and 4), with heavy swing (about 55-65%), velocity variation and slightly late notes. Straight quantising is the most common lo-fi mistake.

KEYS & SCALES
Both major and minor work. The colour comes from extended chords: always use at least 7ths (maj7, m7, dominant 7) and add 9ths for a softer, neo-soul wash.

COMMON PROGRESSIONS
•  ii7 - V7 - Imaj7   (Dm7 - G7 - Cmaj7)  the jazz ii-V-I, the backbone of lo-fi
•  iim7b5 - V7 - im7   (Bm7b5 - E7 - Am7)  minor ii-V-i, melancholic
•  Imaj7 - vi7 - ii7 - V7   (Cmaj7 - Am7 - Dm7 - G7)  jazz turnaround
•  Imaj7 - vi7 - IVmaj7 - V7   (Cmaj7 - Am7 - Fmaj7 - G7)  four-chord loop in 7ths

PRODUCTION TIPS
Hold each chord for a bar or more; lo-fi uses jazz harmony but moves slowly. Vinyl crackle, tape saturation and wobble, and a low-pass on the whole loop are part of the genre, not extras.

LOUDNESS
Typical master: about -14 to -10 LUFS integrated, true peak -1 dBTP or lower.

genres.name: Pop
genres.summary: The vocal is king: everything supports a polished, bright, upfront lead vocal with a controlled low end.

zones.label: Thump
zones.tip: Body of the kick. Boost moderately; pop needs a tight kick, not a huge sub.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Boxiness
zones.tip: Cardboard zone. Cut a few dB to clean up room for the bass and vocal.

zones.label: Click
zones.tip: Attack. A small boost keeps the kick audible in dense arrangements.

tips.eq:
High-pass around 30 Hz.

Pop kicks are tight and controlled: moderate boost at 50-80 Hz, cut boxiness around 300 Hz, and a little click at 3-5 kHz so it's heard under a busy arrangement.

Avoid huge sub boosts and leave room for the bass.
tips.compression:
4:1 ratio, attack 10-30 ms, release ~80 ms, 3-5 dB of reduction for punch.

Many pop mixes also send the drums to a parallel 'smash' bus for extra energy.
tips.sidechain:
Lightly sidechain the bass to the kick (1-3 dB) to keep the low end clean.

Dance-pop uses more obvious pumping on synths and pads.
tips.reverb: Little or none directly on the kick. A shared drum-room reverb on a send (high-passed) adds space to the whole kit.
tips.delay: Not typical on the kick.
tips.gain: Peaks around -12 to -8 dBFS. Balance kick and bass first, then bring the vocal up so it sits clearly on top.

zones.label: Body
zones.tip: Weight of the snare. Boost if thin.

zones.label: Boxiness
zones.tip: Honky, boxy tone. A cut here makes the snare sound more expensive.

zones.label: Crack
zones.tip: Snap. Be careful: this range overlaps the vocal's presence zone.

tips.eq:
High-pass at 80-100 Hz.

Body at 150-250 Hz, cut boxiness around 500 Hz, add crack at 3-6 kHz and a high shelf for air if needed.

Pop snares are bright, but they shouldn't compete with the vocal's 2-5 kHz presence.
tips.compression:
4:1, medium attack (5-20 ms), 3-5 dB of reduction.

Parallel compression adds thickness without losing the hit.
tips.sidechain: Not usually needed.
tips.reverb:
Plate reverb is the classic pop snare sound: 1-2 s decay, 20-40 ms pre-delay.

Gated or huge reverbs for retro/80s pop. Automate more reverb in the chorus for a sense of size.
tips.delay: Occasional slapback or tempo delays as an effect only.
tips.gain: Peaks around -14 to -8 dBFS.

zones.label: Fundamental
zones.tip: Weight of the bass notes. Should feel solid but not boomy.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up. Cut here if the mix feels cloudy.

zones.label: Definition
zones.tip: Note definition, so the bass line is heard on small speakers. Boost or saturate.
zones.tooLittle: Not enough {label}, so this will disappear on phones and laptops. Add saturation/distortion to create harmonics, or boost about {amt} dB around {hz}.

tips.eq:
High-pass around 30 Hz.

Pop bass must be heard on small speakers: boost 700 Hz-1.5 kHz for note definition, or use gentle saturation.

Cut mud around 200-300 Hz and leave space for the kick at its thump frequency.
tips.compression:
Pop bass is very even: 4:1, medium attack, 4-6 dB of reduction.

Two compressors in series (each doing a little) give smooth, natural control.
tips.sidechain: Sidechain to the kick for 1-3 dB of ducking to keep the low end tight.
tips.reverb: Keep the bass dry, and mono below ~150 Hz.
tips.delay: Not used.
tips.gain: Peaks around -12 to -8 dBFS.

zones.label: Rumble
zones.tip: High-pass up to 80-100 Hz to remove rumble and plosive thumps.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter (12-18 dB/oct) and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Muffled zone. Cut if the vocal lacks clarity.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Pop vocals are bright and forward. A broad, gentle boost here.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: Harsh S's. Always de-ess after brightening.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} instead of a static EQ cut. Aim for 3-6 dB of reduction on the S's only.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Glossy sheen. A high shelf of a few dB is common in pop.

tips.eq:
High-pass at 80-100 Hz. Cut mud at 200-400 Hz.

Pop vocals are bright and glossy: a broad presence boost at 2-5 kHz and an air shelf from 10-12 kHz up.

Always de-ess after brightening. Cut harsh resonances narrowly rather than boosting more.
tips.compression:
Heavy but smooth: often two compressors (a fast peak catcher plus a smooth leveller) for 6-10 dB in total.

Add volume automation so every word is equally loud. A pop vocal should feel glued to the front.
tips.sidechain:
Common trick: sidechain the reverb and delay returns to the dry vocal, so the effects bloom only in the gaps.

Also a gentle dynamic-EQ dip in the music at 2-4 kHz while the vocal sings.
tips.reverb:
Plate or hall on a send: 1.5-2.5 s decay, 50-100 ms pre-delay so the words stay clear.

EQ the return (high-pass 300 Hz, low-pass 8 kHz). Use more reverb in choruses and bridges.
tips.delay:
1/4 or dotted-1/8 delays tucked under the vocal, filtered.

Slapback (60-120 ms) for a retro feel. Duck the delay under the vocal (see Sidechain).
tips.gain:
Record peaking around -12 to -6 dBFS.

In the mix the lead vocal is the loudest mid-range element.

zones.label: Clang / body
zones.tip: Low clang and body. Usually high-passed away so hats don't cloud the snare and kick.

zones.label: Harshness
zones.tip: Where hats get harsh and clash with vocals. Cut 1-3 dB if it pierces.
zones.tooMuch: There's {dev} dB more harshness than typical around {hz}. Try a dynamic EQ or a narrow cut of {amt} dB there, and compare with bypass.

zones.label: Sizzle
zones.tip: Shimmer and sparkle. A gentle shelf adds life; too much gets brittle.

tips.eq:
Hats and percussion are clean, tight and supportive. Their job is energy, not attention.

High-pass hats at 300-600 Hz. If they're harsh, cut 1-3 dB around 2-5 kHz; for sparkle, a gentle shelf around 8-10 kHz. Low-pass at 15-18 kHz if they sound fizzy.
tips.compression: Hats rarely need compression. Shape them with velocity and transient shapers instead; light bus compression on all percussion can add glue.
tips.sidechain: Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump. Hats are usually left un-ducked so the groove stays steady.
tips.reverb: Medium spaces work: plates and rooms of 1-2 s on a send, high-passed at 200-400 Hz and low-passed around 8-10 kHz. Keep hat reverb short so it doesn't wash out the groove.
tips.delay: Short 1/16 or 1/8 delays (filtered, low level) create movement on percussion. Ping-pong delays widen hats without making them louder.
tips.gain: Hats and percussion peak around -20 to -12 dBFS. They're usually the quietest drum elements but the busiest.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Leads rarely need this range. High-pass it so the kick and bass stay clean.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up. Cut if the lead sounds cloudy or masks the chords.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Where a lead cuts through. Watch for clashes with the vocal here.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Brightness and shine. Supersaws and plucks live up here too.

tips.eq:
Synth leads and hooks answer the vocal; they should never fight it in the same register.

High-pass at 150-300 Hz (higher if there's a lot going on in the low mids). Find the presence at 1-4 kHz, and if a vocal is present, cut the lead a little where the vocal is strongest.
tips.compression: Synths are already consistent, so compression is optional. Use it for density or saturation for harmonics. OTT-style multiband compression is common in EDM leads.
tips.sidechain: Use light ducking (1-3 dB) from the kick where parts mask it. The groove should feel clean, not pump.
tips.reverb: Medium spaces work: plates and rooms of 1-2 s on a send, high-passed at 200-400 Hz and low-passed around 8-10 kHz.
tips.delay: Tempo-synced delays (1/8, dotted 1/8 or 1/4) on a send. Filter the returns and duck them under the dry lead so the melody stays clear.
tips.gain: Leads peak around -16 to -9 dBFS. They should be clearly heard but sit under the vocal if there is one.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Pads and chords rarely need this. High-pass at 150-300 Hz so kick and bass own the low end.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: The most common mix problem: chords piling up in the low mids. Keep it tidy.

zones.label: Body
zones.tip: The warmth of the chords. Enough to fill, not so much it masks vocals and leads.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Shimmer and width. A gentle shelf can make pads feel expensive.

tips.eq:
Pop chords often use the I-V-vi-IV family. Keep pads and chords below or around the vocal, not on top of it.

High-pass pads and chords at 150-300 Hz, cut mud at 200-500 Hz, and consider a low-pass around 10 kHz on dark pads so they don't fight hats and vocals.
tips.compression: Usually not needed on pads. For stabs, light compression or saturation adds punch. OTT can brighten supersaw chords.

tips.delay: Stereo or ping-pong delays widen chord stabs. Filter and duck them.

zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Honk
zones.tip: Honky, boxy piano tone. Cut 2-4 dB if it sounds cheap.

zones.label: Presence

zones.label: Brilliance

Piano is a pop staple. High-pass at 100-200 Hz and dip 2-4 kHz so the vocal owns the presence range.

zones.label: Presence

zones.label: Air

zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up from stacked vocals. Cut to keep the lead clear.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Keep backing parts a little softer here than the lead vocal.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: Stacked S's get loud fast. De-ess backing vocals harder than the lead.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} rather than a static EQ cut.

Backing vocals, doubles and harmonies widen the chorus. Keep them darker and quieter than the lead.

zones.label: Sub
zones.tip: The deepest low end of the whole mix. Check it on headphones or a sub, and keep it mono.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up across the whole mix: the most common reason mixes sound cloudy.

zones.label: Harshness
zones.tip: Where whole mixes get harsh and tiring. Fix it on the channels if you can.
zones.tooMuch: There's {dev} dB more harshness than typical around {hz}. Try a dynamic EQ or a narrow cut of {amt} dB there, and compare with bypass.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Top-end openness of the mix.

tips.eq:
Pop masters are loud and polished, with a bright, controlled top end.

On the mix bus, EQ in small moves (0.5-2 dB, wide shapes). If one zone needs more than that, fix it on the channel that causes it. Keep everything below about 120 Hz mono.
tips.compression: Mix-bus glue: a slow attack (10-30 ms), auto or 100-300 ms release, ratio 1.5:1-2:1 and only 1-2 dB of gain reduction.
tips.sidechain: Not used on the master. Do sidechain and ducking on the individual channels.
tips.reverb: No reverb on the mix bus. Space belongs on the sends.
tips.delay: No delay on the mix bus.
tips.gain:
Before mastering, leave about 3-6 dB of headroom: peaks around -6 to -3 dBFS on the mix bus, with no limiter.

Typical master loudness for this genre: about -11 to -8 LUFS integrated, with true peak at -1 dBTP or lower.

workflow.title: Genre map
workflow.text: Tempo: Typically 100-130 BPM (ballads slower). The goal: the vocal is king: everything supports a polished, bright, upfront lead vocal with a controlled low end. Decide what job each section has before reaching for processors.

workflow.title: Reference listening
workflow.text: Pick two references: one for groove and one for mix tone. Level-match them before judging your track.

workflow.title: Session template
workflow.text: Create groups for drums, bass, music, hook/vocal and FX. Add a reference track and two sends before writing.

workflow.title: Core rhythm
workflow.text: Build the groove around drums and a chord bed that support the vocal. Keep it simple until the pocket works.

workflow.title: Drum sound choice
workflow.text: Choose kick, snare/clap and hats by role. Tune or swap before stacking processing.

workflow.title: Bass foundation
workflow.text: Use a tight, consistent bass as the low-end anchor. Make the note length and rhythm serve the kick.

workflow.title: Hook identity
workflow.text: Use the vocal melody and chorus hook as the part people remember. Mute it to test whether the track loses identity.

workflow.title: Arrangement sketch
workflow.text: Duplicate the loop across a timeline, then remove elements for intro, breakdown, build, drop/chorus and outro.

workflow.title: Energy curve
workflow.text: Use density, filter movement, automation and drum fills to create lift. Avoid adding layers just because a section feels empty.

workflow.title: Transition design
workflow.text: Use reverse tails, short fills, risers, mutes and reverb throws. A transition should explain the next section.

workflow.title: Kick and bass balance
workflow.text: Set kick and bass before mixing anything else. If these fight, no amount of mastering will save the track.

workflow.title: Sidechain or ducking
workflow.text: Use sidechain only where it creates space or groove. Set release musically, not just visually.

workflow.title: EQ cleanup
workflow.text: High-pass support parts, cut mud in context, and protect the midrange that carries the hook.

workflow.title: Compression
workflow.text: Use compression for control, groove and density. If the part gets smaller, slow the attack or reduce gain reduction.

workflow.title: Saturation
workflow.text: Add harmonics where the part needs to translate on smaller speakers. Gain-match before deciding it sounds better.

workflow.title: Stereo width
workflow.text: Keep the foundation centred. Put width in pads, textures, FX, doubles and support layers.

workflow.title: Reverb
workflow.text: Short spaces add placement. Long spaces add drama. Automate sends so the drop/groove stays focused.

workflow.title: Delay
workflow.text: Use timed delays for call-and-response, vocal chops, fills and ear candy. Filter delay returns to avoid clutter.

workflow.title: Automation pass
workflow.text: Automate one thing per section: filter, send, mute, width, distortion, pitch or macro movement.

workflow.title: Sound design resampling
workflow.text: Print vocal and chorus moments to audio so the arrangement becomes editable and stable.

workflow.title: Vocal or sample space
workflow.text: Leave a pocket for the lead element. If vocals are coming later, mix the beat with that space protected.

workflow.title: Bus processing
workflow.text: Process groups lightly. Drums can take clip/saturation; music can take glue; FX returns can take EQ and ducking.

workflow.title: Loudness prep
workflow.text: Don't chase loudness until the low end and arrangement are stable. Loud masters expose weak balance.

workflow.title: Export checklist
workflow.text: Export the full mix, an instrumental where useful, and a rough master. Name files with BPM, key and version.

workflow.title: Phone check
workflow.text: The groove, hook and vocal space should survive on a phone. Add harmonics if the bass disappears.

workflow.title: Mono check
workflow.text: Collapse to mono and listen for missing hooks or weak drums. Fix phase before widening.

workflow.title: Beginner mistakes
workflow.text: Too many layers, too much reverb, no arrangement contrast, and mixing before the core idea works.

workflow.title: Practice drill
workflow.text: Make a 90-second Pop sketch using only drums, bass, chords, one vocal and two automation moves.

workflow.title: Advanced drill
workflow.text: Build a second version focused on the chorus lift and compare which arrangement keeps energy better.

workflow.title: Release habit
workflow.text: Finish a rough version, write three notes, fix those only, then move on. Completion builds taste faster than endless tweaking.

TEMPO
Typically 100-130 BPM (ballads slower)

GROOVE & DRUMS
Clean, tight drums that support the vocal: kick and snare backbeat, with the arrangement building energy into each chorus.

KEYS & SCALES
Pop uses both major and minor keys. Choose the key that suits the singer's range. Transposing a progression is the easy way to fit a voice.

COMMON PROGRESSIONS
•  I - V - vi - IV   (C - G - Am - F)  the 'four-chord song', the most common pop loop
•  vi - IV - I - V   (Am - F - C - G)  the same chords starting on the minor, more emotional
•  I - vi - IV - V   (C - Am - F - G)  the 50s/doo-wop progression
•  IV - V - vi - I   (F - G - Am - C)  increasingly common in pop since about 2010

PRODUCTION TIPS
I, IV, V and vi are the most common chords in pop. Variety usually comes from rhythm, melody and production rather than complex harmony.

LOUDNESS
Typical master: about -11 to -8 LUFS integrated, true peak -1 dBTP or lower.

genres.name: House
genres.summary: Groove, kick/bass weight, chord stabs, vocal hooks and clean mix energy.

zones.label: Sub thump
zones.tip: The kick's fundamental, the engine of the track. Keep it clean; carve the bass around it.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Boxiness
zones.tip: Mud zone. Cutting here gives a tighter, more club-ready kick.

zones.label: Punch
zones.tip: Click and punch that cut through the synths.

tips.eq:
High-pass at 20-30 Hz.

In house the kick is the loudest, most important element. Make sure its fundamental (usually 45-70 Hz) is clean. Cut boxiness at 250-500 Hz.

Carve the bass around the kick, not the other way round.
tips.compression:
Kick samples are usually ready to use. For loudness, reach for saturation or a clipper rather than heavy compression.

If you do compress: slow attack (20-30 ms) to keep the punch.
tips.sidechain:
The kick is the sidechain source for almost everything: bass (deep ducking, 6-12 dB), pads, synths, even reverb returns. That pumping groove is part of the genre.

Use a muted 'ghost kick' track or a volume-shaper plugin for consistent pumping.
tips.reverb: Kick stays dry and mono. Reverb on the kick muddies the groove.
tips.delay: None.
tips.gain: The kick is your reference: peaks around -8 to -5 dBFS. Build everything else relative to it.

zones.label: Low body
zones.tip: Usually high-passed away in house so the clap doesn't fight the kick and bass.

zones.label: Clap
zones.tip: Where a clap's character lives.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Shine. A high shelf makes claps sparkle on big systems.

tips.eq:
High-pass at 150-200 Hz so it doesn't fight the kick and bass.

Claps live around 1-3 kHz; add air above 8 kHz for shine.

Layered claps: EQ each layer into a different range.
tips.compression: Light. Transient shapers are often more useful than compressors for claps.
tips.sidechain: Not usually ducked: it lands on beats 2 and 4, between the kicks.
tips.reverb:
Claps love reverb in house: short to medium plate or room, 0.8-1.5 s, high-passed.

Big reverb tails for breakdowns and builds.
tips.delay: 1/8 or 1/16 delays on claps add groove. Filter them heavily.
tips.gain: Peaks around -14 to -10 dBFS, under the kick.

zones.label: Sub (mono)
zones.tip: Keep it mono. If it clashes with the kick's fundamental, sidechain or dip it.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Kick clash
zones.tip: Mid-bass build-up that blurs the kick. Clean it out.

zones.label: Character
zones.tip: Growl and character, so the bass is heard in clubs and on phones. Saturation works well here.
zones.tooLittle: Not enough {label}, so this will disappear on phones and laptops. Add saturation/distortion to create harmonics, or boost about {amt} dB around {hz}.

tips.eq:
High-pass around 30 Hz. Keep everything below ~120 Hz mono.

Cut the bass where the kick's fundamental sits if they clash.

For synth basses, add character at 800 Hz-2 kHz with saturation so the bass is heard on every system.
tips.compression: Synth basses are usually stable. Use light compression or limiting for consistency.
tips.sidechain: Essential: deep sidechain (6-12 dB) from the kick, attack ~0-5 ms, release timed to the tempo so the bass swells back between kicks.
tips.reverb: No reverb on the sub. A small amount on filtered mid/high bass layers is fine.
tips.delay: Not on the sub. A short, filtered delay on mid-range bass layers can add movement.
tips.gain:
Peaks around -10 to -6 dBFS.

Kick and bass together should still leave about 6 dB of headroom on your master.

zones.label: Low cut
zones.tip: High-pass harder than in pop (120-200 Hz). The kick and bass need the space.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter (12-18 dB/oct) and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Cut if the vocal blurs into the synths.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Helps the vocal cut through a dense, wide mix.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: De-ess, especially before big reverbs, or S's will splash.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} instead of a static EQ cut. Aim for 3-6 dB of reduction on the S's only.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Bright, airy vocals suit dance music.

tips.eq:
High-pass more aggressively than in pop (120-200 Hz): the kick and bass need that space.

Boost presence at 2-5 kHz and air from 10 kHz up. Thin, bright vocals cut through a dense dance mix.
tips.compression:
Heavy compression for consistency (6-10 dB).

Vocal chops are often limited hard and treated like an instrument.
tips.sidechain:
Light ducking from the kick (1-3 dB) can make the vocal pump with the track.

Sidechain the reverb and delay returns to the vocal so the words stay clear.

Big and wide: halls or plates, 2-4 s, 50-100 ms pre-delay. Lush reverb is part of the genre, especially in breakdowns.

De-ess before the reverb.
tips.delay:
Tempo-synced 1/4, dotted-1/8 or ping-pong delays are standard.

Filter the returns and duck them under the dry vocal.
tips.gain: Peaks around -12 to -6 dBFS.

zones.tooMuch: There's {dev} dB more harshness than typical around {hz}. Try a dynamic EQ or a narrow cut of {amt} dB there, and compare with bypass.

workflow.title: Genre map
workflow.text: Tempo: 120-128 BPM (124-128 is the classic sweet spot; deep house 118-124). The goal: groove, kick/bass weight, chord stabs, vocal hooks and clean mix energy. Decide what job each section has before reaching for processors.

workflow.title: Reference listening
workflow.text: Pick two references: one for groove and one for mix tone. Level-match them before judging your track.

workflow.title: Session template
workflow.text: Create groups for drums, bass, music, hook/vocal and FX. Add a reference track and two sends before writing.

workflow.title: Core rhythm
workflow.text: Build the groove around a four-on-the-floor kick and offbeat hats. Keep it simple until the pocket works.

workflow.title: Drum sound choice
workflow.text: Choose kick, snare/clap and hats by role. Tune or swap before stacking processing.

workflow.title: Bass foundation
workflow.text: Use a warm bassline as the low-end anchor. Make the note length and rhythm serve the kick.

workflow.title: Hook identity
workflow.text: Use piano or organ stabs or vocal chops as the part people remember. Mute it to test whether the track loses identity.

workflow.title: Arrangement sketch
workflow.text: Duplicate the loop across a timeline, then remove elements for intro, breakdown, build, drop/chorus and outro.

workflow.title: Energy curve
workflow.text: Use density, filter movement, automation and drum fills to create lift. Avoid adding layers just because a section feels empty.

workflow.title: Transition design
workflow.text: Use reverse tails, short fills, risers, mutes and reverb throws. A transition should explain the next section.

workflow.title: Kick and bass balance
workflow.text: Set kick and bass before mixing anything else. If these fight, no amount of mastering will save the track.

workflow.title: Sidechain or ducking
workflow.text: Use sidechain only where it creates space or groove. Set release musically, not just visually.

workflow.title: EQ cleanup
workflow.text: High-pass support parts, cut mud in context, and protect the midrange that carries the hook.

workflow.title: Compression
workflow.text: Use compression for control, groove and density. If the part gets smaller, slow the attack or reduce gain reduction.

workflow.title: Saturation
workflow.text: Add harmonics where the part needs to translate on smaller speakers. Gain-match before deciding it sounds better.

workflow.title: Stereo width
workflow.text: Keep the foundation centred. Put width in pads, textures, FX, doubles and support layers.

workflow.title: Reverb
workflow.text: Short spaces add placement. Long spaces add drama. Automate sends so the drop/groove stays focused.

workflow.title: Delay
workflow.text: Use timed delays for call-and-response, vocal chops, fills and ear candy. Filter delay returns to avoid clutter.

workflow.title: Automation pass
workflow.text: Automate one thing per section: filter, send, mute, width, distortion, pitch or macro movement.

workflow.title: Sound design resampling
workflow.text: Print sidechain-pump and club mixdown moments to audio so the arrangement becomes editable and stable.

workflow.title: Vocal or sample space
workflow.text: Leave a pocket for the lead element. If vocals are coming later, mix the beat with that space protected.

workflow.title: Bus processing
workflow.text: Process groups lightly. Drums can take clip/saturation; music can take glue; FX returns can take EQ and ducking.

workflow.title: Loudness prep
workflow.text: Don't chase loudness until the low end and arrangement are stable. Loud masters expose weak balance.

workflow.title: Export checklist
workflow.text: Export the full mix, an instrumental where useful, and a rough master. Name files with BPM, key and version.

workflow.title: Phone check
workflow.text: The groove, hook and vocal space should survive on a phone. Add harmonics if the bass disappears.

workflow.title: Mono check
workflow.text: Collapse to mono and listen for missing hooks or weak drums. Fix phase before widening.

workflow.title: Beginner mistakes
workflow.text: Too many layers, too much reverb, no arrangement contrast, and mixing before the core idea works.

workflow.title: Practice drill
workflow.text: Make a 90-second House sketch using only drums, bass, one hook and two automation moves.

workflow.title: Advanced drill
workflow.text: Build a second version focused on a filtered breakdown and compare which arrangement keeps energy better.

workflow.title: Release habit
workflow.text: Finish a rough version, write three notes, fix those only, then move on. Completion builds taste faster than endless tweaking.

theory.groove: Four-on-the-floor kick, clap or snare on 2 and 4, open hats on every offbeat, 16th shakers. Chord stabs and bass often play in the gaps between each other, a call-and-response that creates groove.
theory.keys: House leans on minor keys (A minor and its relatives are very common), with jazzy minor 7th and 9th chords. Gospel-style major lifts appear in classic Chicago house.
theory.tips: Use Rhodes, organ, piano or warm pads for chords, and try different voicings of the same chord in a row. Deep-house basslines roll (root, root, 5th, root) with a little glide between notes.

genres.theoryText:
TEMPO
120-128 BPM (124-128 is the classic sweet spot; deep house 118-124)

GROOVE & DRUMS
Four-on-the-floor kick, clap or snare on 2 and 4, open hats on every offbeat, 16th shakers. Chord stabs and bass often play in the gaps between each other, a call-and-response that creates groove.

KEYS & SCALES
House leans on minor keys (A minor and its relatives are very common), with jazzy minor 7th and 9th chords. Gospel-style major lifts appear in classic Chicago house.

COMMON PROGRESSIONS
•  i7 - bVII - bVI - V7   (Am7 - G - F - E7)  classic minor vamp, gospel-influenced
•  i7 - v7 - iv7   (Am7 - Em7 - Dm7)  simple deep-house minor 7ths
•  IV - I   (F - C)  gospel house lift (major)
•  i - bVII - bVI - bVII   (Am - G - F - G)  funky four-chord loop

PRODUCTION TIPS
Use Rhodes, organ, piano or warm pads for chords, and try different voicings of the same chord in a row. Deep-house basslines roll (root, root, 5th, root) with a little glide between notes.

LOUDNESS
Typical master: about -9 to -6 LUFS integrated, true peak -1 dBTP or lower.

genres.name: UK Garage
genres.bpm: 130-135 BPM for classic 2-step (UKG overall 130-138; speed garage 138-142)
genres.summary: Swing, shuffled drums, sub movement, chopped vocals and tight low-end space.

zones.label: Thump
zones.tip: Kick weight. Short and tight so the rolling sub moves around it.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Boxiness
zones.tip: Clean this out for a tight, shuffled groove.

zones.label: Click
zones.tip: Snap that keeps the 2-step pattern crisp.

tips.eq:
The 2-step kick skips beats, so each hit counts: weight at 50-80 Hz, click at 2.5-5 kHz, cut boxiness at 200-400 Hz. Keep the tail short.

Classic 2-step placement: kick on 16th-steps 1 and 11, snare on 5 and 13, then add about 55-58% swing.
tips.compression: Light; slow attack for punch. Swing and shuffle come from programming, not processing.
tips.sidechain: Duck the rolling sub from the kick (3-6 dB, short release) for tight low-end space.
tips.reverb: None or a tiny room.
tips.delay: Not used.
tips.gain: Peaks around -9 to -6 dBFS.

zones.label: Body
zones.tip: Snare/rim body. Garage snares are crisp, not huge.

zones.label: Crack
zones.tip: Crisp rimshot and snare snap that drives the shuffle.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Shine on rims and hats.

tips.eq:
Garage uses crisp snares, rimshots and ghost snares. High-pass at 150-200 Hz, crack at 2-5 kHz.

Ghost snares should be quiet and dull (low-pass them) so they add swing without clutter.
tips.compression: Light. Use velocity and swing to shape the groove rather than compression.
tips.sidechain: Not ducked.
tips.reverb: Short rooms and plates (0.5-1 s) to keep the groove tight.
tips.delay: Short 1/16 delays on rims add shuffle.
tips.gain: Peaks around -13 to -8 dBFS; ghost snares 10-15 dB quieter.

zones.label: Sub
zones.tip: The rolling sub: the heartbeat of garage. Mono, moving, clean.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Overlap with kick and organ bass. Keep it tidy.

zones.label: Organ / growl
zones.tip: Organ bass and sub-harmonics that make it heard on small speakers.
zones.tooLittle: Not enough {label}, so this will disappear on phones and laptops. Add saturation/distortion to create harmonics, or boost about {amt} dB around {hz}.

tips.eq: Rolling sub: a sine or near-sine with glides between notes, mono below ~120 Hz. For organ basses, keep the 500 Hz-1.5 kHz bite and high-pass the organ layer above the sub.
tips.compression: Light compression or a limiter so sub notes are even.
tips.sidechain: Duck from the kick (3-6 dB) so the 2-step kick punches through.
tips.reverb: None on the sub.
tips.delay: Not used.
tips.gain: Peaks around -9 to -5 dBFS.

zones.label: Rumble
zones.tip: High-pass up to ~120 Hz to remove rumble and plosives.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter (12-18 dB/oct) and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Muffled, boxy zone. Cut a few dB if the vocal lacks clarity.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Clarity and intelligibility. A gentle broad boost helps the words cut through.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: Harsh S's live here. De-ess rather than EQ.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} instead of a static EQ cut. Aim for 3-6 dB of reduction on the S's only.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Sheen and openness. A gentle high shelf.

tips.eq:
Garage vocals are R&B-style leads and pitched, chopped samples. High-pass at 100-150 Hz, presence at 2-5 kHz, air above 10 kHz.

For vocal chops, pitch-shift and re-sequence them to the swing.
tips.compression: Smooth and consistent (6-10 dB). Chops can be limited harder.
tips.sidechain: Duck reverb and delay returns under the dry vocal.
tips.reverb: Short-to-medium plates. Keep it tight so the swing stays clear.
tips.delay: 1/8 and dotted-1/8 delays on chops add bounce.
tips.gain: Peaks around -12 to -6 dBFS.

zones.label: Clang / body
zones.tip: Low clang and body. Usually high-passed away so hats don't cloud the snare and kick.

zones.label: Harshness
zones.tip: Where hats get harsh and clash with vocals. Cut 1-3 dB if it pierces.
zones.tooMuch: There's {dev} dB more harshness than typical around {hz}. Try a dynamic EQ or a narrow cut of {amt} dB there, and compare with bypass.

zones.label: Sizzle
