genres.theoryText:
TEMPO
130-135 BPM for classic 2-step (UKG overall 130-138; speed garage 138-142)

GROOVE & DRUMS
2-step: the kick skips the regular quarter notes, typically on 16th-steps 1 and 11, with the snare on 5 and 13 (beats 2 and 4). Open hats on the offbeats, swung 16th closed hats. Swing of about 55-58% on 16ths is what makes it garage rather than house.

KEYS & SCALES
Minor keys with soulful extensions: 7ths, 9ths and sus chords on organ (M1-style), Rhodes or piano.

COMMON PROGRESSIONS
•  i7 - iv7   (Am7 - Dm7)  two-chord soulful vamp
•  i9 - bVII - bVI   (Am9 - G - F)  minor lift with extensions
•  iim7b5 - V7 - i   (Bm7b5 - E7 - Am)  R&B-style minor turnaround

PRODUCTION TIPS
Chop and pitch vocals and lock them to the swing. Bass is subby and repetitive, often a rolling sub or organ bass that talks with the kick.

LOUDNESS
Typical master: about -9 to -6 LUFS integrated, true peak -1 dBTP or lower.

genres.name: Techno
genres.summary: Repetition with movement, kick/bass pressure, percussion detail, texture and long-form energy control.

zones.label: Sub thump
zones.tip: The engine of the track. Clean and powerful.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Boxiness
zones.tip: Clean this out. Long techno kicks build mud quickly.

zones.label: Punch
zones.tip: Attack that keeps the kick driving through dense percussion.

tips.eq:
Kick layering is a key element: a sub/body layer (45-65 Hz) plus a top/click layer (2-5 kHz), each high-passed or low-passed so they don't overlap.

High-pass at 25 Hz and cut boxiness at 250-500 Hz.
tips.compression: Usually saturation and clipping rather than compression. If compressing, slow attack (20-30 ms) to keep the transient.
tips.sidechain: The kick ducks the rumble bass (and often everything else). Hypnotic pumping is part of the groove.
tips.reverb:
The classic 'rumble': send the kick to a long, dark reverb, then distort, low-pass and sidechain that return. That's your rumble bass. The kick itself stays dry.

Many producers use a convolution reverb for this and tune the result to the track's root note.
tips.delay: Not on the kick itself.
tips.gain: Peaks around -8 to -5 dBFS. The kick is the reference for every other level.

zones.label: Low body
zones.tip: Usually high-passed so claps don't cloud the kick and rumble.

zones.label: Clap
zones.tip: Where claps and snares cut through.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Sizzle and noise. Industrial textures can live here too.

tips.eq: Techno uses claps, rims and metallic percussion more than big snares. High-pass at 150-250 Hz; character lives at 1-3 kHz and above.
tips.compression: Light; use transient shapers and saturation for industrial grit.
tips.sidechain: Sometimes ducked lightly from the kick so the groove locks.
tips.reverb: Claps with reverb are a techno staple: medium plate or hall, high-passed. Automate the send for tension.
tips.delay: 1/8 and 1/16 delays on percussion loops create hypnotic movement. Filter them and automate feedback for tension.
tips.gain: Peaks around -15 to -10 dBFS, under the kick.

zones.label: Rumble
zones.tip: Rumble bass. Felt pressure that moves with the kick. Keep it mono.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Kick clash
zones.tip: Rumble and kick body collide here. Keep it clean.

zones.label: Texture
zones.tip: Distortion and movement that make the rumble audible.
zones.tooLittle: Not enough {label}, so this will disappear on phones and laptops. Add saturation/distortion to create harmonics, or boost about {amt} dB around {hz}.

tips.eq:
Rumble bass: keep everything below ~120 Hz mono, low-pass the rumble around 200-400 Hz, and cut where it clashes with the kick's fundamental.

Filter movement is the main tool: slowly automate a low-pass to build and release energy.
tips.compression: Saturation and distortion more than compression. Industrial texture comes from parallel distortion.
tips.sidechain: Essential: deep ducking from the kick (6-12 dB) so kick and rumble alternate.
tips.reverb: The rumble often IS a reverb (see the Kick reverb tip). Keep its low end mono and ducked.
tips.delay: Short, filtered delays on mid bass stabs for hypnotic movement.
tips.gain: Peaks around -10 to -6 dBFS.

zones.label: Rumble
zones.tip: High-pass hard (150-250 Hz). The kick and rumble own the low end.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter (12-18 dB/oct) and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Muffled, boxy zone. Cut a few dB if the vocal lacks clarity.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Clarity and intelligibility. A gentle broad boost helps the words cut through.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: Harsh S's live here. De-ess rather than EQ.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} instead of a static EQ cut. Aim for 3-6 dB of reduction on the S's only.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Sheen and openness. A gentle high shelf.

tips.eq: Techno vocals are usually short samples, spoken words or chants. High-pass at 150-250 Hz and shape them as texture.
tips.compression: Heavy compression or distortion for industrial character.
tips.sidechain: Duck under the kick so vocals pump with the groove.
tips.reverb: Dark, long reverbs and gated spaces. Automate for tension.
tips.delay: Filtered, high-feedback delays for hypnotic repetition. Automate feedback and filter cut-off as tension tools.
tips.gain: Peaks around -14 to -8 dBFS.

zones.label: Clang / body
zones.tip: Low clang and body. Usually high-passed away so hats don't cloud the snare and kick.

zones.label: Harshness
zones.tip: Where hats get harsh and clash with vocals. Cut 1-3 dB if it pierces.
zones.tooMuch: There's {dev} dB more harshness than typical around {hz}. Try a dynamic EQ or a narrow cut of {amt} dB there, and compare with bypass.

zones.label: Sizzle
zones.tip: Shimmer and sparkle. A gentle shelf adds life; too much gets brittle.

tips.eq:
Driving 16th hats, rides and metallic percussion carry the energy. Automate filters and decay for movement.

High-pass hats at 300-600 Hz. If they're harsh, cut 1-3 dB around 2-5 kHz; for sparkle, a gentle shelf around 8-10 kHz. Low-pass at 15-18 kHz if they sound fizzy.
tips.compression: Hats rarely need compression. Shape them with velocity and transient shapers instead; light bus compression on all percussion can add glue.
tips.sidechain: Sidechain pumping is part of the genre's groove: duck from the kick (6-12 dB, attack ~0 ms, release timed to the tempo, roughly 100-200 ms). Hats are usually left un-ducked so the groove stays steady.
tips.reverb: Medium spaces work: plates and rooms of 1-2 s on a send, high-passed at 200-400 Hz and low-passed around 8-10 kHz. Keep hat reverb short so it doesn't wash out the groove.
tips.delay: Short 1/16 or 1/8 delays (filtered, low level) create movement on percussion. Ping-pong delays widen hats without making them louder.
tips.gain: Hats and percussion peak around -20 to -12 dBFS. They're usually the quietest drum elements but the busiest.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Leads rarely need this range. High-pass it so the kick and bass stay clean.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up. Cut if the lead sounds cloudy or masks the chords.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Where a lead cuts through. Watch for clashes with the vocal here.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Brightness and shine. Supersaws and plucks live up here too.

tips.eq:
Leads are minimal: acid lines, one-note sequences and stabs. Repetition with slow change is the point.

High-pass at 150-300 Hz (higher if there's a lot going on in the low mids). Find the presence at 1-4 kHz, and if a vocal is present, cut the lead a little where the vocal is strongest.
tips.compression: Synths are already consistent, so compression is optional. Use it for density or saturation for harmonics. OTT-style multiband compression is common in EDM leads.
tips.sidechain: Sidechain pumping is part of the genre's groove: duck from the kick (6-12 dB, attack ~0 ms, release timed to the tempo, roughly 100-200 ms).
tips.reverb: Medium spaces work: plates and rooms of 1-2 s on a send, high-passed at 200-400 Hz and low-passed around 8-10 kHz.
tips.delay: Tempo-synced delays (1/8, dotted 1/8 or 1/4) on a send. Filter the returns and duck them under the dry lead so the melody stays clear.
tips.gain: Leads peak around -16 to -9 dBFS. They should be clearly heard but sit under the vocal if there is one.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Pads and chords rarely need this. High-pass at 150-300 Hz so kick and bass own the low end.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: The most common mix problem: chords piling up in the low mids. Keep it tidy.

zones.label: Body
zones.tip: The warmth of the chords. Enough to fill, not so much it masks vocals and leads.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Shimmer and width. A gentle shelf can make pads feel expensive.

tips.eq:
Dark minor or Phrygian stabs, often just two or three notes, hitting off the beat.

High-pass pads and chords at 150-300 Hz, cut mud at 200-500 Hz, and consider a low-pass around 10 kHz on dark pads so they don't fight hats and vocals.
tips.compression: Usually not needed on pads. For stabs, light compression or saturation adds punch. OTT can brighten supersaw chords.
tips.sidechain: Sidechain pumping is part of the genre's groove: duck from the kick (6-12 dB, attack ~0 ms, release timed to the tempo, roughly 100-200 ms).
tips.reverb: Medium spaces work: plates and rooms of 1-2 s on a send, high-passed at 200-400 Hz and low-passed around 8-10 kHz. Pads can take more reverb than anything else in the mix.
tips.delay: Stereo or ping-pong delays widen chord stabs. Filter and duck them.
tips.gain: Chords and pads peak around -18 to -10 dBFS. They support; they're rarely the loudest element.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Rumble and boom. High-pass so the bass owns the low end.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Honk
zones.tip: Honky, boxy piano tone. Cut 2-4 dB if it sounds cheap.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Definition. A small dip here makes room for the vocal.

zones.label: Brilliance
zones.tip: Sparkle on the hammers. A gentle boost for brightness.

tips.eq:
Rare in most techno; dub techno uses filtered chord stabs drenched in delay.

In a busy mix, high-pass piano at 100-200 Hz, cut honk at 500 Hz-1 kHz, and dip 2-4 kHz slightly so the vocal owns the presence range. Boost 5-8 kHz for brilliance.
tips.compression: Gentle compression (2-4 dB, medium attack) evens out dynamics. Keep it light on expressive parts.
tips.sidechain: Sidechain pumping is part of the genre's groove: duck from the kick (6-12 dB, attack ~0 ms, release timed to the tempo, roughly 100-200 ms).
tips.reverb: Medium spaces work: plates and rooms of 1-2 s on a send, high-passed at 200-400 Hz and low-passed around 8-10 kHz.
tips.delay: Subtle delays add depth; long filtered delays suit ambient and lo-fi keys.
tips.gain: Keys peak around -16 to -9 dBFS depending on how central they are to the track.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Rumble and boom. High-pass so the bass stays clear.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Boom / mud
zones.tip: Boominess and boxiness. Cut 2-4 dB if the guitar masks the bass or vocal.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Pick attack and definition. Where a guitar cuts through.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Shimmer and string sparkle, especially on acoustics.

tips.eq:
Rare. Treat it as texture if used.

High-pass at 80-100 Hz (acoustics from 60 Hz; push higher until it thins, then back off). Cut 200-500 Hz if it's boomy; add presence at 1.5-5 kHz and air at 8-12 kHz.
tips.compression: Light compression (2-4 dB) for strummed parts; more for funky, rhythmic riffs.
tips.sidechain: Sidechain pumping is part of the genre's groove: duck from the kick (6-12 dB, attack ~0 ms, release timed to the tempo, roughly 100-200 ms).
tips.reverb: Medium spaces work: plates and rooms of 1-2 s on a send, high-passed at 200-400 Hz and low-passed around 8-10 kHz.
tips.delay: Slapback or tempo delays add space; long delays and volume swells create ambient textures.
tips.gain: Guitars peak around -16 to -9 dBFS.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Backing vocals and chops don't need this. High-pass at 150-300 Hz.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up from stacked vocals. Cut to keep the lead clear.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Keep backing parts a little softer here than the lead vocal.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: Stacked S's get loud fast. De-ess backing vocals harder than the lead.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} rather than a static EQ cut.

tips.eq:
Short vocal samples and chants, treated as texture with heavy effects.

High-pass backing vocals and chops at 150-300 Hz, cut mud at 200-400 Hz, and keep them slightly darker than the lead so it stays in front.
tips.compression: Compress harder than the lead (6-10 dB) so stacks stay even and sit behind it.
tips.sidechain: Duck backing vocals 1-3 dB under the lead vocal if they compete. Sidechain pumping is part of the genre's groove: duck from the kick (6-12 dB, attack ~0 ms, release timed to the tempo, roughly 100-200 ms).
tips.reverb: Medium spaces work: plates and rooms of 1-2 s on a send, high-passed at 200-400 Hz and low-passed around 8-10 kHz. Backing parts can take more reverb than the lead, which pushes them behind it.
tips.delay: Filtered stereo delays widen chops and harmonies. Keep them lower than the lead's delay.
tips.gain: Backing vocals and chops peak around -18 to -10 dBFS, below the lead vocal.

zones.label: Sub
zones.tip: The deepest low end of the whole mix. Check it on headphones or a sub, and keep it mono.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up across the whole mix: the most common reason mixes sound cloudy.

zones.label: Harshness
zones.tip: Where whole mixes get harsh and tiring. Fix it on the channels if you can.
zones.tooMuch: There's {dev} dB more harshness than typical around {hz}. Try a dynamic EQ or a narrow cut of {amt} dB there, and compare with bypass.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Top-end openness of the mix.

tips.eq:
Club-loud with a powerful, clean low end. The kick and rumble must stay punchy.

On the mix bus, EQ in small moves (0.5-2 dB, wide shapes). If one zone needs more than that, fix it on the channel that causes it. Keep everything below about 120 Hz mono.
tips.compression: Mix-bus glue: a slow attack (10-30 ms), auto or 100-300 ms release, ratio 1.5:1-2:1 and only 1-2 dB of gain reduction.
tips.sidechain: Not used on the master. Do sidechain and ducking on the individual channels.
tips.reverb: No reverb on the mix bus. Space belongs on the sends.
tips.delay: No delay on the mix bus.
tips.gain:
Before mastering, leave about 3-6 dB of headroom: peaks around -6 to -3 dBFS on the mix bus, with no limiter.

Typical master loudness for this genre: about -9 to -6 LUFS integrated, with true peak at -1 dBTP or lower.

Streaming services turn loud masters down: Spotify plays at about -14 LUFS by default (-11 LUFS in its 'loud' mode), Apple Music at about -16 LUFS. So mastering louder than the genre needs only costs you punch. Compare with a level-matched reference.

workflow.title: Reference listening
workflow.text: Pick two references: one for groove and one for mix tone. Level-match them before judging your track.

workflow.title: Session template
workflow.text: Create groups for drums, bass, music, hook/vocal and FX. Add a reference track and two sends before writing.

workflow.title: Core rhythm
workflow.text: Build the groove around kick layering and rumble bass. Keep it simple until the pocket works.

workflow.title: Drum sound choice
workflow.text: Choose kick, snare/clap and hats by role. Tune or swap before stacking processing.

workflow.title: Bass foundation
workflow.text: Use a rumble bass driven by filter movement as the low-end anchor. Make the note length and rhythm serve the kick.

workflow.title: Hook identity
workflow.text: Use a percussion loop or tension automation as the part people remember. Mute it to test whether the track loses identity.

workflow.title: Arrangement sketch
workflow.text: Duplicate the loop across a timeline, then remove elements for intro, breakdown, build, drop/chorus and outro.

workflow.title: Energy curve
workflow.text: Use density, filter movement, automation and drum fills to create lift. Avoid adding layers just because a section feels empty.

workflow.title: Transition design
workflow.text: Use reverse tails, short fills, risers, mutes and reverb throws. A transition should explain the next section.

workflow.title: Kick and bass balance
workflow.text: Set kick and bass before mixing anything else. If these fight, no amount of mastering will save the track.

workflow.title: Sidechain or ducking
workflow.text: Use sidechain only where it creates space or groove. Set release musically, not just visually.

workflow.title: EQ cleanup
workflow.text: High-pass support parts, cut mud in context, and protect the midrange that carries the hook.

workflow.title: Compression
workflow.text: Use compression for control, groove and density. If the part gets smaller, slow the attack or reduce gain reduction.

workflow.title: Saturation
workflow.text: Add harmonics where the part needs to translate on smaller speakers. Gain-match before deciding it sounds better.

workflow.title: Stereo width
workflow.text: Keep the foundation centred. Put width in pads, textures, FX, doubles and support layers.

workflow.title: Reverb
workflow.text: Short spaces add placement. Long spaces add drama. Automate sends so the drop/groove stays focused.

workflow.title: Delay
workflow.text: Use timed delays for call-and-response, vocal chops, fills and ear candy. Filter delay returns to avoid clutter.

workflow.title: Automation pass
workflow.text: Automate one thing per section: filter, send, mute, width, distortion, pitch or macro movement.

genres.name: Trance
genres.bpm: 134-140 BPM (138 is the classic uplifting tempo)
genres.summary: Melody, supersaw emotion, clean kick/bass drive, long builds and dramatic breakdown/release.

zones.label: Thump
zones.tip: Clean, tight kick weight. Short tail so the rolling bass fits between hits.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Boxiness
zones.tip: Clean this out for the wide supersaws.

zones.label: Punch
zones.tip: Hard, clean punch that drives the track.

tips.eq: Trance kicks are tight and punchy with a short tail, so the rolling bass fits between hits. High-pass at 25-30 Hz, weight at 45-70 Hz, punch at 2-5 kHz, cut boxiness at 250-450 Hz.
tips.compression: Kicks are usually pre-processed. Use a clipper for loudness; if compressing, slow attack.
tips.sidechain: Duck the supersaws and pads from the kick (3-6 dB) to keep the drive clean. The rolling bass is usually written between kicks, so it needs less ducking.
tips.reverb: None on the kick.
tips.delay: Not used.
tips.gain: Peaks around -8 to -5 dBFS.

zones.label: Low body
zones.tip: High-pass so claps don't cloud the kick.

zones.label: Clap
zones.tip: Clap/snare snap on 2 and 4.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Shine for the big, open trance sound.

tips.eq: High-pass claps at 150-200 Hz. Snap at 1-4 kHz, air above 8 kHz.
tips.compression: Light; transient shapers work well.
tips.sidechain: Not usually ducked.
tips.reverb: Plate or hall (1-2 s). Bigger in breakdowns and builds.
tips.delay: Snare builds (rolls that speed up from 1/4 to 1/32) are a classic trance move. Automate a high-pass filter and pitch up as the build rises.
tips.gain: Peaks around -14 to -9 dBFS.

zones.label: Sub
zones.tip: Rolling bass fundamental. Mono and tight.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Kick clash
zones.tip: Rolling bass and kick overlap here. Keep it clean.

zones.label: Definition
zones.tip: Note definition so the rolling pattern is heard.
zones.tooLittle: Not enough {label}, so this will disappear on phones and laptops. Add saturation/distortion to create harmonics, or boost about {amt} dB around {hz}.

tips.eq: The rolling bass (usually 16th-note offbeats, avoiding the kick) carries the drive. High-pass at 30 Hz, keep below ~120 Hz mono, add definition at 500 Hz-1.5 kHz.
tips.compression: Light; synth basses are consistent.
tips.sidechain: Even when written between kicks, a short duck (3-6 dB) from the kick keeps the low end tight.
tips.reverb: None on the sub.
tips.delay: Not on the bass.
tips.gain: Peaks around -10 to -6 dBFS.

zones.label: Rumble
zones.tip: High-pass up to ~150 Hz to remove rumble and plosives.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter (12-18 dB/oct) and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Muffled, boxy zone. Cut a few dB if the vocal lacks clarity.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Clarity and intelligibility. A gentle broad boost helps the words cut through.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: Harsh S's live here. De-ess rather than EQ.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} instead of a static EQ cut. Aim for 3-6 dB of reduction on the S's only.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Airy, emotional vocals suit uplifting trance. A high shelf, then de-ess.

tips.eq: High-pass at 120-200 Hz, boost presence and air: trance vocals are bright, airy and emotional, sitting above the supersaws.
tips.compression: Smooth two-stage compression (6-10 dB).
tips.sidechain: Duck the supersaw stack 2-4 dB under the vocal, and duck the vocal reverb/delay returns under the dry vocal.
tips.reverb: Huge halls and plates, especially in the long breakdown. Automate size and send level with the emotion.
tips.delay: Dotted-1/8 and 1/4 delays are classic. Filter and duck them.
tips.gain: Peaks around -12 to -6 dBFS.

zones.label: Clang / body
zones.tip: Low clang and body. Usually high-passed away so hats don't cloud the snare and kick.

zones.label: Harshness
zones.tip: Where hats get harsh and clash with vocals. Cut 1-3 dB if it pierces.
zones.tooMuch: There's {dev} dB more harshness than typical around {hz}. Try a dynamic EQ or a narrow cut of {amt} dB there, and compare with bypass.

zones.label: Sizzle
zones.tip: Shimmer and sparkle. A gentle shelf adds life; too much gets brittle.

tips.eq:
909-style offbeat open hats and 16th shakers drive the groove. Straight timing, no swing.

High-pass hats at 300-600 Hz. If they're harsh, cut 1-3 dB around 2-5 kHz; for sparkle, a gentle shelf around 8-10 kHz. Low-pass at 15-18 kHz if they sound fizzy.
tips.compression: Hats rarely need compression. Shape them with velocity and transient shapers instead; light bus compression on all percussion can add glue.
tips.sidechain: Sidechain pumping is part of the genre's groove: duck from the kick (6-12 dB, attack ~0 ms, release timed to the tempo, roughly 100-200 ms). Hats are usually left un-ducked so the groove stays steady.
tips.reverb: This genre is wet and wide: halls and plates of 2-4 s with 30-80 ms pre-delay, ducked under the dry signal so the groove stays clear. Keep hat reverb short so it doesn't wash out the groove.
tips.delay: Short 1/16 or 1/8 delays (filtered, low level) create movement on percussion. Ping-pong delays widen hats without making them louder.
tips.gain: Hats and percussion peak around -20 to -12 dBFS. They're usually the quietest drum elements but the busiest.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Leads rarely need this range. High-pass it so the kick and bass stay clean.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up. Cut if the lead sounds cloudy or masks the chords.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Where a lead cuts through. Watch for clashes with the vocal here.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Brightness and shine. Supersaws and plucks live up here too.

tips.eq:
The supersaw or pluck lead is the emotional centre. Wide, bright, and full of reverb and delay.

High-pass at 150-300 Hz (higher if there's a lot going on in the low mids). Find the presence at 1-4 kHz, and if a vocal is present, cut the lead a little where the vocal is strongest.
tips.compression: Synths are already consistent, so compression is optional. Use it for density or saturation for harmonics. OTT-style multiband compression is common in EDM leads.
tips.sidechain: Sidechain pumping is part of the genre's groove: duck from the kick (6-12 dB, attack ~0 ms, release timed to the tempo, roughly 100-200 ms).
tips.reverb: This genre is wet and wide: halls and plates of 2-4 s with 30-80 ms pre-delay, ducked under the dry signal so the groove stays clear.
tips.delay: Tempo-synced delays (1/8, dotted 1/8 or 1/4) on a send. Filter the returns and duck them under the dry lead so the melody stays clear.
tips.gain: Leads peak around -16 to -9 dBFS. They should be clearly heard but sit under the vocal if there is one.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Pads and chords rarely need this. High-pass at 150-300 Hz so kick and bass own the low end.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: The most common mix problem: chords piling up in the low mids. Keep it tidy.

zones.label: Body
zones.tip: The warmth of the chords. Enough to fill, not so much it masks vocals and leads.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Shimmer and width. A gentle shelf can make pads feel expensive.

tips.eq:
Minor progressions like i-VI-III-VII (Am-F-C-G) on wide supersaws, often with 16th arpeggios.

High-pass pads and chords at 150-300 Hz, cut mud at 200-500 Hz, and consider a low-pass around 10 kHz on dark pads so they don't fight hats and vocals.
tips.compression: Usually not needed on pads. For stabs, light compression or saturation adds punch. OTT can brighten supersaw chords.
tips.sidechain: Sidechain pumping is part of the genre's groove: duck from the kick (6-12 dB, attack ~0 ms, release timed to the tempo, roughly 100-200 ms).
tips.reverb: This genre is wet and wide: halls and plates of 2-4 s with 30-80 ms pre-delay, ducked under the dry signal so the groove stays clear. Pads can take more reverb than anything else in the mix.
tips.delay: Stereo or ping-pong delays widen chord stabs. Filter and duck them.
tips.gain: Chords and pads peak around -18 to -10 dBFS. They support; they're rarely the loudest element.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Rumble and boom. High-pass so the bass owns the low end.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Honk
zones.tip: Honky, boxy piano tone. Cut 2-4 dB if it sounds cheap.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Definition. A small dip here makes room for the vocal.

zones.label: Brilliance
zones.tip: Sparkle on the hammers. A gentle boost for brightness.

tips.eq:
Piano often opens the breakdown before the supersaws take over.

In a busy mix, high-pass piano at 100-200 Hz, cut honk at 500 Hz-1 kHz, and dip 2-4 kHz slightly so the vocal owns the presence range. Boost 5-8 kHz for brilliance.
tips.compression: Gentle compression (2-4 dB, medium attack) evens out dynamics. Keep it light on expressive parts.
tips.sidechain: Sidechain pumping is part of the genre's groove: duck from the kick (6-12 dB, attack ~0 ms, release timed to the tempo, roughly 100-200 ms).
tips.reverb: This genre is wet and wide: halls and plates of 2-4 s with 30-80 ms pre-delay, ducked under the dry signal so the groove stays clear.
tips.delay: Subtle delays add depth; long filtered delays suit ambient and lo-fi keys.
tips.gain: Keys peak around -16 to -9 dBFS depending on how central they are to the track.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Rumble and boom. High-pass so the bass stays clear.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Boom / mud
zones.tip: Boominess and boxiness. Cut 2-4 dB if the guitar masks the bass or vocal.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Pick attack and definition. Where a guitar cuts through.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Shimmer and string sparkle, especially on acoustics.

tips.eq:
Occasional (Balearic and vocal trance). Keep it clean and spacious.

High-pass at 80-100 Hz (acoustics from 60 Hz; push higher until it thins, then back off). Cut 200-500 Hz if it's boomy; add presence at 1.5-5 kHz and air at 8-12 kHz.
tips.compression: Light compression (2-4 dB) for strummed parts; more for funky, rhythmic riffs.
tips.sidechain: Sidechain pumping is part of the genre's groove: duck from the kick (6-12 dB, attack ~0 ms, release timed to the tempo, roughly 100-200 ms).
tips.reverb: This genre is wet and wide: halls and plates of 2-4 s with 30-80 ms pre-delay, ducked under the dry signal so the groove stays clear.
tips.delay: Slapback or tempo delays add space; long delays and volume swells create ambient textures.
tips.gain: Guitars peak around -16 to -9 dBFS.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Backing vocals and chops don't need this. High-pass at 150-300 Hz.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up from stacked vocals. Cut to keep the lead clear.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Keep backing parts a little softer here than the lead vocal.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: Stacked S's get loud fast. De-ess backing vocals harder than the lead.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} rather than a static EQ cut.

tips.eq:
Vocal pads, choirs and chops add emotion in breakdowns.

High-pass backing vocals and chops at 150-300 Hz, cut mud at 200-400 Hz, and keep them slightly darker than the lead so it stays in front.
tips.compression: Compress harder than the lead (6-10 dB) so stacks stay even and sit behind it.
tips.sidechain: Duck backing vocals 1-3 dB under the lead vocal if they compete. Sidechain pumping is part of the genre's groove: duck from the kick (6-12 dB, attack ~0 ms, release timed to the tempo, roughly 100-200 ms).
tips.reverb: This genre is wet and wide: halls and plates of 2-4 s with 30-80 ms pre-delay, ducked under the dry signal so the groove stays clear. Backing parts can take more reverb than the lead, which pushes them behind it.
tips.delay: Filtered stereo delays widen chops and harmonies. Keep them lower than the lead's delay.
tips.gain: Backing vocals and chops peak around -18 to -10 dBFS, below the lead vocal.

zones.label: Sub
zones.tip: The deepest low end of the whole mix. Check it on headphones or a sub, and keep it mono.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up across the whole mix: the most common reason mixes sound cloudy.

zones.label: Harshness
zones.tip: Where whole mixes get harsh and tiring. Fix it on the channels if you can.
zones.tooMuch: There's {dev} dB more harshness than typical around {hz}. Try a dynamic EQ or a narrow cut of {amt} dB there, and compare with bypass.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Top-end openness of the mix.

tips.eq:
Loud and wide, with a clean kick and controlled high end on the supersaws.

On the mix bus, EQ in small moves (0.5-2 dB, wide shapes). If one zone needs more than that, fix it on the channel that causes it. Keep everything below about 120 Hz mono.
tips.compression: Mix-bus glue: a slow attack (10-30 ms), auto or 100-300 ms release, ratio 1.5:1-2:1 and only 1-2 dB of gain reduction.
tips.sidechain: Not used on the master. Do sidechain and ducking on the individual channels.
tips.reverb: No reverb on the mix bus. Space belongs on the sends.
tips.delay: No delay on the mix bus.
tips.gain:
Before mastering, leave about 3-6 dB of headroom: peaks around -6 to -3 dBFS on the mix bus, with no limiter.

Typical master loudness for this genre: about -9 to -6 LUFS integrated, with true peak at -1 dBTP or lower.

Streaming services turn loud masters down: Spotify plays at about -14 LUFS by default (-11 LUFS in its 'loud' mode), Apple Music at about -16 LUFS. So mastering louder than the genre needs only costs you punch. Compare with a level-matched reference.

workflow.title: Genre map
workflow.text: Tempo: 134-140 BPM (138 is the classic uplifting tempo). The goal: melody, supersaw emotion, clean kick/bass drive, long builds and dramatic breakdown/release. Decide what job each section has before reaching for processors.

workflow.title: Reference listening
workflow.text: Pick two references: one for groove and one for mix tone. Level-match them before judging your track.

workflow.title: Session template
workflow.text: Create groups for drums, bass, music, hook/vocal and FX. Add a reference track and two sends before writing.

workflow.title: Core rhythm
workflow.text: Build the groove around the kick, a rolling bass and a pluck motif. Keep it simple until the pocket works.

workflow.title: Drum sound choice
workflow.text: Choose kick, snare/clap and hats by role. Tune or swap before stacking processing.

workflow.title: Bass foundation
workflow.text: Use a rolling offbeat bass that leaves room for the kick as the low-end anchor. Make the note length and rhythm serve the kick.

workflow.title: Hook identity
workflow.text: Use the supersaw stack or pluck motif as the part people remember. Mute it to test whether the track loses identity.

workflow.title: Arrangement sketch
workflow.text: Duplicate the loop across a timeline, then remove elements for intro, breakdown, build, drop/chorus and outro.

workflow.title: Energy curve
workflow.text: Use density, filter movement, automation and drum fills to create lift. Avoid adding layers just because a section feels empty.

workflow.title: Transition design
workflow.text: Use reverse tails, short fills, risers, mutes and reverb throws. A transition should explain the next section.

workflow.title: Kick and bass balance
workflow.text: Set kick and bass before mixing anything else. If these fight, no amount of mastering will save the track.

workflow.title: Sidechain or ducking
workflow.text: Use sidechain only where it creates space or groove. Set release musically, not just visually.

workflow.title: EQ cleanup
workflow.text: High-pass support parts, cut mud in context, and protect the midrange that carries the hook.

workflow.title: Compression
workflow.text: Use compression for control, groove and density. If the part gets smaller, slow the attack or reduce gain reduction.

workflow.title: Saturation
workflow.text: Add harmonics where the part needs to translate on smaller speakers. Gain-match before deciding it sounds better.

workflow.title: Stereo width
workflow.text: Keep the foundation centred. Put width in pads, textures, FX, doubles and support layers.

workflow.title: Reverb
workflow.text: Short spaces add placement. Long spaces add drama. Automate sends so the drop/groove stays focused.

workflow.title: Delay
workflow.text: Use timed delays for call-and-response, vocal chops, fills and ear candy. Filter delay returns to avoid clutter.

workflow.title: Automation pass
workflow.text: Automate one thing per section: filter, send, mute, width, distortion, pitch or macro movement.

workflow.title: Sound design resampling
workflow.text: Print supersaw and riser moments to audio so the arrangement becomes editable and stable.

workflow.title: Vocal or sample space
workflow.text: Leave a pocket for the lead element. If vocals are coming later, mix the beat with that space protected.

workflow.title: Bus processing
workflow.text: Process groups lightly. Drums can take clip/saturation; music can take glue; FX returns can take EQ and ducking.

workflow.title: Loudness prep
workflow.text: Don't chase loudness until the low end and arrangement are stable. Loud masters expose weak balance.

workflow.title: Export checklist
workflow.text: Export the full mix, an instrumental where useful, and a rough master. Name files with BPM, key and version.

workflow.title: Phone check
workflow.text: The groove, hook and vocal space should survive on a phone. Add harmonics if the bass disappears.

workflow.title: Mono check
workflow.text: Collapse to mono and listen for missing hooks or weak drums. Fix phase before widening.

workflow.title: Beginner mistakes
workflow.text: Too many layers, too much reverb, no arrangement contrast, and mixing before the core idea works.

workflow.title: Practice drill
workflow.text: Make a 90-second Trance sketch using only drums, rolling bass, one lead and two automation moves.

workflow.title: Advanced drill
workflow.text: Build a second version focused on the long breakdown and drop release and compare which arrangement keeps energy better.

workflow.title: Release habit
workflow.text: Finish a rough version, write three notes, fix those only, then move on. Completion builds taste faster than endless tweaking.

genres.theoryText:
TEMPO
134-140 BPM (138 is the classic uplifting tempo)

GROOVE & DRUMS
Four-on-the-floor kick with no swing, clap on 2 and 4, open hats on the offbeats, 16th shakers. A rolling offbeat bass plays in the gaps between kicks and is sidechained so the track pumps.

KEYS & SCALES
Trance overwhelmingly favours minor keys (A, D, F# and G minor are common), lifting to major chords for the emotional moments.

COMMON PROGRESSIONS
•  i - VI - III - VII   (Am - F - C - G)  the classic uplifting trance progression
•  i - bVI - bVII - i   (Am - F - G - Am)  anthemic minor lift
•  i - iv - bVI - bVII   (Fm - Bbm - Db - Eb)  emotional breakdown progression
•  i - bVI - bVII - V   (Am - F - G - E)  tension before the drop

PRODUCTION TIPS
Let a 16th-note arpeggio trace the chords, and save the full supersaw lead for after the long breakdown and build.

LOUDNESS
Typical master: about -9 to -6 LUFS integrated, true peak -1 dBTP or lower.

genres.name: Drum & Bass
genres.bpm: 172-176 BPM (174 is the standard); the groove feels half-time, around 86-88 BPM
genres.summary: Fast drums, controlled sub, aggressive bass layers, clear midrange and loud-but-clean energy.

zones.label: Thump
zones.tip: Body of the kick. In DnB it's tight and short so it doesn't smear the sub at 170 BPM.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Boxiness
zones.tip: Clean this out. Fast tempos turn low-mid boom into mud quickly.

zones.label: Click
zones.tip: Snap that cuts through heavy reese basses.

tips.eq:
High-pass at 30-35 Hz. DnB kicks are short and punchy: the body at 50-80 Hz, a strong click at 3-6 kHz so it cuts through the bass.

Cut boxiness at 250-450 Hz. Keep the kick tail short. At 170 BPM, long tails clash with the sub.
tips.compression: Fast attack can kill the punch, so use 10-20 ms attack, fast release, 3-4 dB. Many producers rely on the drum bus clipper rather than compressing each hit.
tips.sidechain: Sub separation is a key idea in the guides: duck the sub under the kick (fast attack, 50-80 ms release, 3-6 dB), or carve the sub with a dynamic EQ keyed from the kick.
tips.reverb: Almost none on the kick. A very short room on the whole drum bus can add glue.
tips.delay: Not used on the kick.
tips.gain: Peaks around -9 to -5 dBFS. Kick and snare are the loudest drum elements; the snare is usually as loud as or louder than the kick.

zones.label: Body
zones.tip: Snare weight is a defining DnB sound. This is the 'thwack' body.

zones.label: Boxiness
zones.tip: Honk and box. Cut to keep the midrange clear for the reese.

zones.label: Crack
zones.tip: The crack that drives the 2 and 4. Needs to cut through everything.

tips.eq:
The DnB snare is huge: body at 180-250 Hz, crack at 1.5-4 kHz. High-pass at 100-150 Hz and cut boxiness around 500 Hz.

Layer a clap or a short noise burst for extra crack if it disappears behind the bass.
tips.compression:
Parallel compression on the drum bus is classic DnB: blend a heavily squashed copy under the dry drums.

On the snare itself: medium attack, 3-5 dB.
tips.sidechain: Some producers duck the reese mid-bass a little (1-3 dB) from the snare so it punches through.
tips.reverb: A short, bright plate or room (0.5-1 s) on a send. Keep tails short at 170 BPM so they don't wash over the next hit.
tips.delay: Occasional 1/8 delay throws on the last snare before a drop.
tips.gain: Peaks around -8 to -4 dBFS. Snare weight is part of the genre's energy.

zones.label: Sub
zones.tip: The clean sine sub. Keep it mono and on its own layer, separate from the reese.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Where sub and reese overlap the kick body. Carve it out.

zones.label: Reese / mids
zones.tip: The moving, detuned reese or neuro layer. This is where the character lives.
zones.tooLittle: Not enough {label}, so this will disappear on phones and laptops. Add saturation/distortion to create harmonics, or boost about {amt} dB around {hz}.

tips.eq:
Split your bass into two layers: a clean sine sub below ~100 Hz (mono) and a reese/neuro layer above it, high-passed at 100-150 Hz.

This 'sub separation' lets you distort and move the mid layer as much as you want without wrecking the low end.
tips.compression: Sub: a limiter or light compression for consistency. Reese/neuro layer: heavy processing is normal (OTT, multiband compression, distortion chains), then EQ after it.
tips.sidechain: Duck the whole bass group from the kick and snare (fast attack, 60-100 ms release). This is the key move for a clean, loud DnB low end.
tips.reverb: None on the sub. A tiny bit on a high-passed copy of the reese for space in breakdowns only.
tips.delay: Not on the sub. Short, filtered delays on neuro stabs can add movement in the drop.
tips.gain: Peaks around -9 to -5 dBFS for the bass group. Leave headroom for the drum bus clipping.

zones.label: Rumble
zones.tip: High-pass higher than in pop (120-180 Hz). The sub and reese need that space.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter (12-18 dB/oct) and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Muffled, boxy zone. Cut a few dB if the vocal lacks clarity.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Clarity and intelligibility. A gentle broad boost helps the words cut through.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: Harsh S's live here. De-ess rather than EQ.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} instead of a static EQ cut. Aim for 3-6 dB of reduction on the S's only.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Sheen and openness. A gentle high shelf.

tips.eq: DnB vocals (MCs, liquid vocals, samples) need to cut through a very dense mix. High-pass at 120-180 Hz, cut mud at 200-400 Hz, and boost presence at 2-5 kHz.
tips.compression: Heavy and consistent: 6-10 dB in two stages. MC vocals are often compressed hard for energy.
tips.sidechain: Duck the reese mid-bass 2-3 dB under the vocal, or use a dynamic EQ dip at 1-3 kHz on the bass keyed from the vocal.
tips.reverb: Liquid DnB: lush plates and halls. Neuro/jump-up: short and dry. Always high-pass the reverb return.
tips.delay: 1/4 and dotted-1/8 delays on line endings, filtered and ducked under the dry vocal.
tips.gain: Peaks around -12 to -6 dBFS.

zones.label: Clang / body
zones.tip: Low clang and body. Usually high-passed away so hats don't cloud the snare and kick.

zones.label: Harshness
zones.tip: Where hats get harsh and clash with vocals. Cut 1-3 dB if it pierces.
zones.tooMuch: There's {dev} dB more harshness than typical around {hz}. Try a dynamic EQ or a narrow cut of {amt} dB there, and compare with bypass.

zones.label: Sizzle
zones.tip: Shimmer and sparkle. A gentle shelf adds life; too much gets brittle.

tips.eq:
Fast, busy hats and break ghost-notes give DnB its roll. Keep them crisp but not harsh at 174 BPM.

High-pass hats at 300-600 Hz. If they're harsh, cut 1-3 dB around 2-5 kHz; for sparkle, a gentle shelf around 8-10 kHz. Low-pass at 15-18 kHz if they sound fizzy.
tips.compression: Hats rarely need compression. Shape them with velocity and transient shapers instead; light bus compression on all percussion can add glue.
tips.sidechain: Moderate ducking (3-6 dB) from the kick and snare keeps the drums punching through. Hats are usually left un-ducked so the groove stays steady.
tips.reverb: Keep spaces small and controlled: short rooms and plates (0.5-1.2 s), high-passed at 200-400 Hz. Keep hat reverb short so it doesn't wash out the groove.
tips.delay: Short 1/16 or 1/8 delays (filtered, low level) create movement on percussion. Ping-pong delays widen hats without making them louder.
tips.gain: Hats and percussion peak around -20 to -12 dBFS. They're usually the quietest drum elements but the busiest.

zones.label: Low end
zones.tip: Leads rarely need this range. High-pass it so the kick and bass stay clean.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up. Cut if the lead sounds cloudy or masks the chords.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Where a lead cuts through. Watch for clashes with the vocal here.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Brightness and shine. Supersaws and plucks live up here too.

tips.eq:
Leads range from liquid pads to neuro stabs. They sit above the reese, not in it.

High-pass at 150-300 Hz (higher if there's a lot going on in the low mids). Find the presence at 1-4 kHz, and if a vocal is present, cut the lead a little where the vocal is strongest.
tips.compression: Synths are already consistent, so compression is optional. Use it for density or saturation for harmonics. OTT-style multiband compression is common in EDM leads.
tips.sidechain: Moderate ducking (3-6 dB) from the kick and snare keeps the drums punching through.
tips.reverb: Keep spaces small and controlled: short rooms and plates (0.5-1.2 s), high-passed at 200-400 Hz.
tips.delay: Tempo-synced delays (1/8, dotted 1/8 or 1/4) on a send. Filter the returns and duck them under the dry lead so the melody stays clear.

zones.label: Mud

zones.label: Body

workflow.title: Genre map
workflow.text: Tempo: 172-176 BPM (174 is the standard); the groove feels half-time, around 86-88 BPM. The goal: fast drums, controlled sub, aggressive bass layers, clear midrange and loud-but-clean energy. Decide what job each section has before reaching for processors.

workflow.title: Reference listening
workflow.text: Pick two references: one for groove and one for mix tone. Level-match them before judging your track.

workflow.title: Session template
workflow.text: Create groups for drums, bass, music, hook/vocal and FX. Add a reference track and two sends before writing.

workflow.title: Core rhythm
workflow.text: Build the groove around kick and snare weight and amen break edits. Keep it simple until the pocket works.

workflow.title: Drum sound choice
workflow.text: Choose kick, snare/clap and hats by role. Tune or swap before stacking processing.

workflow.title: Bass foundation
workflow.text: Use a clean sub (kept separate from the reese/neuro layers) as the low-end anchor. Make the note length and rhythm serve the kick.

workflow.title: Hook identity
workflow.text: Use reese bass layers or neuro movement as the part people remember. Mute it to test whether the track loses identity.

workflow.title: Arrangement sketch
workflow.text: Duplicate the loop across a timeline, then remove elements for intro, breakdown, build, drop/chorus and outro.

workflow.title: Energy curve
workflow.text: Use density, filter movement, automation and drum fills to create lift. Avoid adding layers just because a section feels empty.

workflow.title: Transition design
workflow.text: Use reverse tails, short fills, risers, mutes and reverb throws. A transition should explain the next section.

workflow.title: Kick and bass balance
workflow.text: Set kick and bass before mixing anything else. If these fight, no amount of mastering will save the track.

workflow.title: Sidechain or ducking
workflow.text: Use sidechain only where it creates space or groove. Set release musically, not just visually.

workflow.title: EQ cleanup
workflow.text: High-pass support parts, cut mud in context, and protect the midrange that carries the hook.

workflow.title: Compression
workflow.text: Use compression for control, groove and density. If the part gets smaller, slow the attack or reduce gain reduction.

workflow.title: Saturation
workflow.text: Add harmonics where the part needs to translate on smaller speakers. Gain-match before deciding it sounds better.

workflow.title: Stereo width
workflow.text: Keep the foundation centred. Put width in pads, textures, FX, doubles and support layers.

workflow.title: Reverb
workflow.text: Short spaces add placement. Long spaces add drama. Automate sends so the drop/groove stays focused.

workflow.title: Delay
workflow.text: Use timed delays for call-and-response, vocal chops, fills and ear candy. Filter delay returns to avoid clutter.

workflow.title: Automation pass
workflow.text: Automate one thing per section: filter, send, mute, width, distortion, pitch or macro movement.

workflow.title: Sound design resampling
workflow.text: Print neuro bass and drum-break moments to audio so the arrangement becomes editable and stable.

workflow.title: Vocal or sample space
workflow.text: Leave a pocket for the lead element. If vocals are coming later, mix the beat with that space protected.

workflow.title: Bus processing
workflow.text: Process groups lightly. Drums can take clip/saturation; music can take glue; FX returns can take EQ and ducking.

workflow.title: Loudness prep
workflow.text: Don't chase loudness until the low end and arrangement are stable. Loud masters expose weak balance.

workflow.title: Export checklist
workflow.text: Export the full mix, an instrumental where useful, and a rough master. Name files with BPM, key and version.

workflow.title: Phone check
workflow.text: The groove, hook and vocal space should survive on a phone. Add harmonics if the bass disappears.

workflow.title: Mono check
workflow.text: Collapse to mono and listen for missing hooks or weak drums. Fix phase before widening.

workflow.title: Beginner mistakes
workflow.text: Too many layers, too much reverb, no arrangement contrast, and mixing before the core idea works.

workflow.title: Practice drill
workflow.text: Make a 90-second DnB sketch using only drums, bass, one hook and two automation moves.

workflow.title: Advanced drill
workflow.text: Build a second version focused on drop energy and compare which arrangement keeps energy better.

workflow.title: Release habit
workflow.text: Finish a rough version, write three notes, fix those only, then move on. Completion builds taste faster than endless tweaking.

genres.theoryText:
TEMPO
172-176 BPM (174 is the standard); the groove feels half-time, around 86-88 BPM

GROOVE & DRUMS
Two-step pattern: kick on beat 1, snares on beats 2 and 4, with chopped breakbeats (e.g. the Amen break) and ghost hits in between. The snare is bright and cracking and must cut through the reese.

KEYS & SCALES
Mostly minor. Tune the sub and reese precisely to the track's root note; producers even transpose whole tracks a semitone or two to get the kick and bass to sit together.

COMMON PROGRESSIONS
•  i - bVI - bIII - bVII   (Am - F - C - G)  liquid DnB minor progression
•  i - iv   (Am - Dm)  two-chord minor vamp for neuro/jump-up
•  im9 - bVImaj7   (Am9 - Fmaj7)  lush liquid extended chords

PRODUCTION TIPS
Split the low end into two jobs: a clean sine/triangle sub that locks to the kick, and a reese (detuned saws) above it for movement. Never let the sub and reese peak at full level at the same time. Dotted-1/8 delays suit DnB FX sends.

LOUDNESS
Typical master: about -8 to -5 LUFS integrated, true peak -1 dBTP or lower.

tips.delay: Not used.
tips.gain: Peaks around -8 to -5 dBFS. Kick and snare should hit as hard as the bass.

zones.label: Body
zones.tip: The massive half-time snare body. A defining sound of the genre.

zones.label: Boxiness
zones.tip: Honk. Cut so the growls own the mids.

zones.label: Crack
zones.tip: Impact and crack on beat 3. Must cut through the drop.

The half-time snare on beat 3 is the biggest drum hit in the track. Body at 180-260 Hz, crack at 1.5-5 kHz. Layer two or three snares (a body, a crack, a noise tail) and EQ each to its own range.

In riddim, layering the kick on the same beat-3 hit gives the stomping, marching feel.
tips.compression: Heavy. Snares are often clipped or compressed hard (6-10 dB) to stay loud next to the bass. Parallel compression helps.
tips.sidechain: Duck the growl bass 2-4 dB from the snare so the hit punches through.
tips.reverb: Short, bright room or plate (0.5-1.2 s). Big reverb tails only in build-ups and pre-drop tension moments.
tips.delay: Delay throws on the pre-drop snare are a classic tension move.
tips.gain: Peaks around -7 to -4 dBFS. Often as loud as the kick.

zones.label: Sub anchor
zones.tip: Clean sine sub. Mono, steady, separate from the growls.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Low-mid build-up from distorted layers. Clean it so the sub stays clear.

zones.label: Growl / mids
zones.tip: Where growls, wubs and riddim basses live. The main character of the drop.
zones.tooLittle: Not enough {label}, so this will disappear on phones and laptops. Add saturation/distortion to create harmonics, or boost about {amt} dB around {hz}.

zones.label: Presence

TEMPO
140 BPM is the centre (138-145; riddim 140-150), felt as half-time ~70 BPM

GROOVE & DRUMS
Kick on beat 1 (sometimes also the 'and' of 2), snare or clap hard on beat 3, the defining half-time backbeat. Sparse hats and percussion with swung or triplet feels. Space between hits is where the bass lives.

KEYS & SCALES
Minor keys (A, D, C and F minor are common). Riddim is built on one tight, metallic bass motif that loops and evolves through modulation rather than changing notes.

COMMON PROGRESSIONS
•  i - iv - i   (Fm - Bbm - Fm)  simple minor drop harmony
•  i - bVI - bVII   (Am - F - G)  melodic dubstep intros and builds
•  i (pedal)   (one root note, bass call-and-response)  riddim: rhythm over harmony

PRODUCTION TIPS
Keep a separate clean sub and high-pass every growl layer above it. In riddim, layering the kick on the beat-3 snare creates the stomping feel.

LOUDNESS
Typical master: about -7 to -4 LUFS integrated, true peak -1 dBTP or lower.

zones.label: Thump

tips.delay: Not used.
tips.gain: Peaks around -9 to -6 dBFS.

zones.label: Body
zones.tip: Weight of the half-time snare/clap.

zones.label: Crack
zones.tip: Snap of the clap/snare on beat 3.

zones.label: Air
zones.tip: Shine. Future bass snares are bright and polished.

tips.sidechain: Not ducked; it's often the brightest hit in the drop.
tips.reverb: Bright plate or hall (1-2 s) on a send. Snare reverb is a big part of the spacious sound.

tips.gain: Peaks around -10 to -6 dBFS.

zones.label: Sub
zones.tip: Sub support under the chords. Usually a sine following the chord roots.
zones.tooLittle: The low end is {dev} dB weaker than typical for {genre}. Boost about {amt} dB around {hz} with a wide bell or low shelf, or choose a sample with more weight.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Where the chord stack's low notes pile up. Keep it clean.

tips.gain: Peaks around -10 to -6 dBFS.

zones.label: Rumble
zones.tip: High-pass up to ~120 Hz to remove rumble and plosives.
zones.tooMuch: There's low-end rumble below {hi}. Add a high-pass filter (12-18 dB/oct) and raise it until the sound starts to thin out, then back off a little.

zones.label: Mud
zones.tip: Muffled, boxy zone. Cut a few dB if the vocal lacks clarity.

zones.label: Presence
zones.tip: Clarity and intelligibility. A gentle broad boost helps the words cut through.

zones.label: Sibilance
zones.tip: Harsh S's live here. De-ess rather than EQ.
zones.tooMuch: S and T sounds are strong (peaking around {hz}). Use a de-esser set to about {hz} instead of a static EQ cut. Aim for 3-6 dB of reduction on the S's only.

Pitch-shift and formant-shift chops to turn them into melodic instruments.

theory.keys: Major and minor both work; the emotion comes from extended chords (7ths, 9ths, add9) on detuned supersaws.
